t: About
x: ← Project Scroll About About Project Scroll Project Scroll is independent historical research: an online treasure hunt anyone can play, a research desk anyone can hire, and a studio for digital imaging, design, photography, 3D LiDAR, animation and video. All of it runs on one rule. Every clue is true, and every answer is in the record. Who we are Project Scroll is run by an independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, and who trained in visual communications. The research behind that writing is the same research we offer you: old certificates, deeds, surveys, county histories and newspapers, read line by line and compared until they agree, or until we can say exactly why they don’t. What we offer Professional research. Lost ancestors, family histories and registers, family legends tested against the record, forgotten places, maps and land surveys, heirlooms, lodges and old societies, historical research for authors, films and local groups, and a second pair of eyes on anything you mean to publish. Research services . Imaging, design and video. Digital imaging of photographs, documents, maps and heirlooms; imaging analysis of faded ink, damaged pages and the details in old photographs; image creation and restoration; graphic design for family books, charts, covers and keepsakes; web design for families, societies and small businesses; photography; and video production, from family-history films to recorded interviews. 3D and living documents. Landscapes modeled in three dimensions from public LiDAR elevation surveys, 3D animations and fly-throughs, every reconstruction labeled as one, and living documents: research papers, timelines and family records that keep growing as new evidence turns up, with every change dated. The studio . Every commission starts with an honest first read: what can be done, and what it will take, before you commit to anything. What we believe The record decides. Not the family tree online, not the story everybody tells, not what we hoped to find. Every statement is marked. You can always see whether a fact comes from a document, a book, a family story or our own reading. How we mark the evidence . Gaps are shown, not filled. An honest “not yet known” is worth more than a confident guess. Corrections are welcome. If you know better, tell us. The record is bigger than any one of us. Places and people are respected. The hunt never asks anyone to dig, to disturb a grave or a mound, or to go looking for anyone’s home. When we get something wrong We will. When a reader or a new document shows that a page of this site is mistaken, we change the page, date the change on it, and say what was wrong, rather than quietly replacing the words, and list it on the corrections page . A case that was called solved on a bad reading is reopened and says so. If you have found an error, write to research@projectscroll.com or tell us on Facebook; corrections are credited to the person who sent them, by name or not, as they prefer. The record behind this site The dates on the scroll, the person of the month and the then-and-now maps are built from the same sources the hunt asks you to open: Rogers (1875), Mathews (1882), Glover (1906), the 1860 wall map at the Library of Congress, and Michigan death certificates at the Archives of Michigan. Where a page of this site makes a claim, the source is on the page or one click away. If it is not, that is a correction we owe. Where it started Project Scroll began in Cassopolis, Michigan , with a few questions the county history couldn’t answer. It doesn’t stop there. The hunt and the desk now take on questions from anywhere the records reach. t: Accessibility
x: ← Project Scroll For every reader Accessibility The hunt is open to anyone, anywhere, and that includes anyone who reads with a keyboard, a screen reader, a magnifier, captions or a steady page. We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA, and we test every change against them. What is built in Keyboard. Every link, button, filter, map control and dialog works from the keyboard. A “Skip to the content” link is the first thing on every page. Press / or Ctrl K to search. Screen readers. Pages use real headings, landmarks and labels. Pictures carry text descriptions; decorative ornaments are hidden from screen readers. Motion. If your device asks for reduced motion, the gold leaf, glints, rolling place names and drawn trails hold still. The Pause all motion switch at the foot of every page does the same on any device, and remembers your choice. Light and dark. The site follows your device, and the moon button switches by hand. Text and controls are checked for contrast in both. Listening. The Listen buttons read a section aloud with your device’s own voice. Text size. Zoom to 200% or more and the page reflows to one column without sideways scrolling. Print. Every page prints cleanly, without the animations and controls. What is harder, and how we help The deep-zoom maps in the map room are pictures served by the Library of Congress. Their town names and directories are given in text beside them, and we will read any part of a map for you on request. Old handwriting and print. Certificates and book pages are shown as pictures. Where a page is the subject of a case, its key lines are transcribed in the text; ask, and we will transcribe any page you need. Facebook. Clues are posted on Facebook, whose accessibility is Meta’s. Every case also has its own page here. Tell us If anything on Project Scroll is hard to use, write to research@projectscroll.com with the page and what happened. We answer, and we fix what we can. t: Your tin badges
x: ← Project Scroll Your field book Your tin badges In the winter of 1846–47, two hundred badges of the “Ancient and Honorable Order” were worn at a ball in Cassopolis. Not one is known to survive. Here you can earn your own: twenty-three of them: twenty for the things you do as you explore the site, two for keeping the hunt going, and one for cracking a case, with five ranks on the way from Candidate to Keeper of the Hall. Say the word Somewhere on every page of this site, a line is written in code. Turn it with the cipher wheel in the hunter’s toolkit , and it will tell you what to do. The word The second line You broke the first. Here is a harder one, and the cipher wheel alone will not open it. Look at the wheel’s other setting. GSV HVXLMW DLIW RH XSZIGVI. ML DSVVO DROO GFIM RG. SLOW RG GL Z NRIILI. The second word Carry your ledger Your badges, followed cases and notebook live only in this browser. To carry them to another device, take your ledger with you: a small file, made here, that Project Scroll on another device can read back. Nothing is sent to us. Bring a ledger back Your charter Every badge earned. You may print your charter: type your name as you want it written, then print. Your name Your charter is made on this device. Nothing is sent anywhere. Project Scroll Charter of the Hall Know all by these presents that having read the walls, followed the record, broken both ciphers and earned every one of the tin badges, is hereby received as Keeper of the Hall with all the honor and none of the dignity that any such title has ever carried. Every clue is true. Every answer is in the record. Your badges are kept only in this browser, on this device. Nobody else can see them, and we never receive them. t: Benton Harbor, Michigan: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Berrien County, Michigan Benton Harbor Benton Harbor was dug into being. In 1859 Sterne Brunson, Charles Hull and Henry C. Morton planned a canal from the east bank of the St. Joseph River across the marsh, and the first ship canal, 25 feet wide, was finished in 1862. The village laid out beside it in 1860 was called Brunson's Harbor; in 1865 it took the name of Benton Township instead. It was chartered as a village in 1869 and became a city in 1891, the busy fruit-shipping twin of St. Joseph across the river. At a glance Founded village laid out, 1860; ship canal finished, 1862, and widened in 1868; village charter approved April 3, 1869; city, 1891 Name first Brunson's Harbor, at Sterne Brunson's request; renamed in 1865 for Benton Township, which had been named in 1837 for Senator Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri, a friend of Michigan's admission as a state The canal Ellis's 1880 history prints a Centennial address of July 4, 1876, telling how a canal was talked of in 1834 and revived in 1859, and how Martin Green was hired to dig it; the canal and the railroad pulled the district's trade to the Harbor The oldest house Eleazar Morton and his son Henry built the Morton House in 1849; four generations of Mortons lived there until 1936, and it is now the city's history museum Fruit by 1880 Ellis called the village the market-town for most of the people of the district; the old fruit market in the "flats" stood until urban renewal in 1967, and the market now trades in Benton Township County seat no; the county seat of Berrien County is St. Joseph, across the river Worth a visit Morton House Museum , 501 Territorial Road, Benton Harbor. The house Eleazar and Henry Morton built in 1849, the oldest building in Benton Harbor, now a museum of the city's settlement, trade and people. State historical marker. Fidelity Building , 162 Pipestone St., Benton Harbor. A downtown business building. National Register, 2002. Blossomland Bridge , M-63 over the St. Joseph River. The bascule bridge carrying M-63 between Benton Harbor and St. Joseph. National Register, 1999. Where the records are Berrien County's older vital records are kept by the County Records Department at 2100 E. Empire Ave., Benton Township: births and deaths from 1867, marriages from 1831. The Morton House Museum, 501 Territorial Road, calls itself the home of Benton Harbor history. The Palladium, in its many forms, runs from 1868 to the present; long runs are digitized on Newspapers.com and NewspaperArchive (subscription). The History Center at Courthouse Square, 313 N. Cass St., Berrien Springs, keeps a research library for the whole county. Ellis's History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties (1880) covers the village under Benton Township. Sources Franklin Ellis and Crisfield Johnson, History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (Philadelphia: D. W. Ensign, 1880): Benton Township named for Col. Thomas H. Benton, March 11, 1837; "THE BENTON HARBOR SHIP CANAL" and the 1876 Centennial address (page 219); canal "first but 25 feet wide, and was finished in 1862," enlarged 1868; village laid out 1860, renamed 1865; "shall be known as the village of Benton Harbor" under a charter approved April 3, 1869 (page 220); Sterne Brunson and "The village received the name of Brunson Harbor" (pages 237–238); "the market-town" (page 261) link Wikipedia, "Benton Harbor, Michigan" (founders; 1865 rename for Thomas Hart Benton; city 1891; fruit market) link Michigan History Center, historical marker "The Morton House" (L0037), 501 Territorial Road link Southwest Michigan Tourist Council, "Morton House Museum" link Wikipedia, "National Register of Historic Places listings in Berrien County, Michigan" link Berrien County, "Genealogy" (County Records Department) link ldsgenealogy.com, "Benton Harbor Genealogy" (Palladium runs and where digitized) link Dates and names are from the county histories and official sources listed here. t: Berrien Springs, Michigan: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Berrien County, Michigan Berrien Springs Berrien Springs stands on Wolf's Prairie, a tract of about a thousand acres in a bend of the St. Joseph River. John Pike made the first settlement there in 1829, and the village of Berrien was laid out in 1831. In 1837 the legislature made it the county seat, and the courthouse finished in 1839 still stands on its square, the oldest in Michigan. The seat moved to St. Joseph in 1894, and the old square is now the county's history center. At a glance Founded first settlement by John Pike at Wolf's Prairie, 1829; village of Berrien platted, 1831; post office renamed Berrien Springs, 1836 Name for the county, which was named for John M. Berrien of Georgia, attorney general under President Jackson, 1829–31; "Springs" was added for the mineral springs found near the village County seat from 1837, by an act of February 25 effective May 1, until April 1894, when a county vote moved the seat to St. Joseph; the proprietors gave the county four village lots for its buildings The courthouse built by Gilbert B. Avery and opened in April 1839 at a cost of about $2,500; it is called Michigan's oldest courthouse The first fair the county agricultural society met at the courthouse in February 1850, and the first county fair was held at Berrien Springs in 1851 Pickles the village once called itself the Christmas pickle capital of the world, and its pickle festival was revived in 2021 Worth a visit Berrien Springs Courthouse (History Center at Courthouse Square) , 313 N. Cass St., Berrien Springs. The 1839 courthouse, called Michigan's oldest, with its courtroom restored; the heart of the county history center. National Register, 1970. Old Berrien County Courthouse Complex , Bounded by Cass, Kimmel, Madison and Union Streets, Berrien Springs. The whole courthouse square, with the sheriff's residence and other county buildings of the seat years. National Register, 1982. Where the records are The History Center at Courthouse Square, 313 N. Cass St., run by the Berrien County Historical Association in the old county buildings, opened a research library in the upper floors of the restored sheriff's residence after 2021. Berrien County's older vital records are kept by the County Records Department at 2100 E. Empire Ave., Benton Township: births and deaths from 1867, marriages from 1831. Ellis's History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties (1880) tells the village's story under Oronoko Township, with the names of the first settlers on Wolf's Prairie. Sources Franklin Ellis and Crisfield Johnson, History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (Philadelphia: D. W. Ensign, 1880): "Wolf's Prairie, of about one thousand acres"; "John Pike made the first settlement, at Wolf's Prairie (Berrien Springs)" (page 143); county named for Berrien, who "held the office of Attorney-General under President Jackson, 1829-31" (page 144); act of February 25, 1837, moving the seat to the village, and lots 255, 256, 301 and 302 accepted April 18, 1837 (page 148); agricultural society 1850 and first fair 1851 (page 164); Oronoko Township and Wolf's Prairie settlers (pages 356–358) link Wikipedia, "Berrien Springs, Michigan" (plat 1831; post office renamed 1836; mineral springs; county seat 1837–1894; Christmas pickle) link Wikipedia, "Old Berrien County Courthouse Complex" link Southwest Michigan Tourist Council, "The History Center at Courthouse Square" (313 N Cass St; Berrien County Historical Association, est. 1968) link Wikipedia, "National Register of Historic Places listings in Berrien County, Michigan" link Berrien County, "Genealogy" (County Records Department) link Dates and names are from the county histories and official sources listed here. t: Buchanan, Michigan: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Berrien County, Michigan Buchanan Buchanan grew on McCoy's Creek, which drops about sixty feet on its way to the St. Joseph River and once turned more than a dozen mills. Charles Cowles settled there and built a sawmill in 1833, and the mill man John Hamilton platted the village in 1842. The Michigan Central Railroad came through in 1849, and the village was incorporated in 1858. In 1904 the town talked a Chicago firm into moving here; renamed Clark Equipment in 1916, it made axles and forklift trucks and kept Buchanan at work for decades. At a glance Founded first settled by Charles Cowles, 1833; township organized 1837; village platted by John Hamilton, 1842; incorporated as a village, 1858 Name for James Buchanan of Pennsylvania, later the fifteenth president; Ellis's 1880 history says simply, "The town derived its name from James Buchanan" — the township, organized in 1837, and the village after it Mills about thirteen water mills stood on McCoy's Creek in the 1800s; Pears Mill, built as a flour mill in 1857–58, is the only one left A fire in 1862 fire leveled much of the downtown; merchants rebuilt in brick, and the three-story Union Block, with its upstairs hall, went up in 1863 Industry the George R. Rich Manufacturing Company came from Chicago in 1904–05 with about thirty men; as Clark Equipment it employed nearly 1,300 by 1929 and became a Fortune 500 company County seat no; the county seat of Berrien County is St. Joseph Worth a visit Pears Mill , Downtown Buchanan, south of Front St. between Oak and Days Streets. The flour mill of 1857–58 on McCoy's Creek, the last of the town's water mills, kept by the volunteer Buchanan Preservation Society; open Saturday mornings, Memorial Day to Labor Day. Buchanan Downtown Historic District , Front St. and Main St., Buchanan. The brick Italianate business blocks rebuilt after the 1862 fire. National Register, 2009; state historical marker on Front Street. Union Block , 114 E. Front St., Buchanan. The three-story Italianate block built by John D. Ross and Lorenzo Alexander in 1863, with an event hall on the third floor. National Register, 2007. Where the records are The Buchanan District Library, 128 E. Front St., has scanned and put online almost every issue of the Berrien County Record and Buchanan Record it holds, more than 5,800 issues from 1868 to 1998, with smaller runs of the town's other papers. Berrien County's older vital records are kept by the County Records Department at 2100 E. Empire Ave., Benton Township: births and deaths from 1867, marriages from 1831. The History Center at Courthouse Square, 313 N. Cass St., Berrien Springs, keeps a research library for the county. Ellis's 1880 History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties covers the village under Buchanan Township. Sources Franklin Ellis and Crisfield Johnson, History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (Philadelphia: D. W. Ensign, 1880): first township meeting near the mouth of McCoy's Creek, April 3, 1837, and "The town derived its name from James Buchanan"; "The village of Buchanan was incorporated in 1858" (page 206) link Michigan History Center, historical marker "Buchanan Downtown" (L2276), 2015 (Cowles; more than fifteen mills on McCoy's Creek; Bainton's mill 1857–58, later Pears Mill; Union Block 1863; 1862 fire; George R. t: Cassopolis, Michigan history and records
x: ← Project Scroll Cass County, Michigan Cassopolis, Michigan: its history, in the record Cassopolis is the county seat of Cass County, Michigan, platted in 1831 and named for Lewis Cass, then governor of Michigan Territory. This page gathers what Project Scroll has opened so far on the village and its county: the maps, the county histories, the certificates and the newspapers, with a link to each record where it is held. The village at a glance Founded: platted 1831; chosen as county seat the same year, a compromise between rival settlements. Named for: Lewis Cass (1782–1866), governor of Michigan Territory 1813–31, later Secretary of War and of State. First published histories: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875); Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882); L. H. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County (Chicago, 1906). On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley wall map of Cass County, held by the Library of Congress, carries a plan of the village with lot numbers and owners; you can lay it over today’s streets , and the county’s township sheets of about 1928 are in the map room . Vital records: Michigan death certificates from 1897 are free to read at the Archives of Michigan; here is how to read one . Who kept the village in 1860: two hotels, three merchants and three physicians, engraved beside the Cassopolis plan on the county wall map. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860 · Library of Congress What the hunt has found in Cassopolis The hunt began here, with a joke secret society of 1846 whose story is told in Rogers and Mathews, a village hotel that was hauled across town and turned into a mill, and a doctor who kept a bone. Each is an open case on the case board ; the first two are listed here, and each has its sources free online. Who told Shepard the story of the 1846 lodge? Where did the Union Hotel go when it became a mill? Document of the month: one page of Rogers, 1875, read slowly A field note: one letter, two certificates Next door, 1860 and 1928 Penn Township is the ground just east of the village, with Diamond Lake in its south-west corner and Vandalia on the railroad. Here it is twice: as the 1860 wall map engraved it, and as a plat book drew it about 1928. The square mile sections are the same, so the two line up. Slide across and watch sixty-eight years of owners change hands. 1860 c. 1928 Penn Township, 1860 and about 1928. Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860, Library of Congress · plat book, about 1928, Cass County MIGenWeb A challenge Find the families who stayed Ten surnames are written on this township in both years: on a farm in 1860, and still on the land about 1928. Find them. Slide the map, read the names, and type each one you find. A surname on both maps The hotel corner, thirty years on In 1860 the engraver wrote one word on the block by the court house: HOTEL. Twenty-four years later the Sanborn Map Company drew the same corner building by building, for the insurers. The court house and post office face Broadway, the county jail and the sheriff’s house stand behind them, and across the street stands a hotel under a name the 1860 directory never lists. Is it on the ground where the 1860 hotel stood? Lay the two maps side by side and decide for yourself. Broadway and State, November 1884: the court house and post office, the jail, the county offices and the Exchange House. Pink is brick, yellow is wood. Open the whole sheet , or step through the 1892, 1899 and 1909 editions in the map room. t: Find a grave or an obituary
x: ← Family research Family research, county by county Find a grave or an obituary Where the burial records, obituary indexes and death certificates are for the seven counties of the St. Joseph River valley, and how to ask for a copy. Each entry links to the office or library that holds the record. Fees and hours change: check before you write or go. Cass County, Michigan Burials and cemetery records Township and village clerks / sextons . Most Cass County cemeteries are owned by the townships (or the village/city); burial and lot records sit with the township clerk or sexton. t: Project Scroll for classrooms
x: ← Project Scroll For teachers Project Scroll for classrooms New: the teachers’ pack. A one-day field trip to Cassopolis (the Broadway walk, the Local History Branch and the photo spots), with two printable worksheets: rephotographing an old postcard, and reading an old record. Download the teachers’ pack (PDF) Four ready lessons in local history and map reading, built on the real maps, directories and county histories of the St. Joseph River Valley. Free, nothing to sign up for, and nothing collected from students. Print this page and go. Then and now Grades 3 and up · 40 minutes · Map reading, change over time You need: Seven towns, then and now and a screen or printed copies. Choose a town near your school. Open its page and fade slowly from the old plan to today. List three things that are still there (a street, a square, a river crossing) and three that are gone. Find the street that changed its name, using the challenge on the page. Talk about it: why might a town rename a street? Who decides? Going further: Walk the street, if you can, with the “Where am I?” button on a phone, and photograph what stands there now. Who was in town Grades 4 to 8 · 45 minutes · Primary sources as data, graphs You need: Who was in town and a screen or printed copies. Pick one town’s 1860 or 1861 business directory. Sort the entries into trades: law, medicine, food, building, transport, making things. Make a bar graph of the trades. Which town had the most lawyers? The most shoemakers? Ask: who is missing from a directory that people paid to be listed in? (Most farmers, labourers, women and children.) Going further: Compare two towns, or a directory of today, and write what changed. This day in the valley Grades 6 to 12 · 45 minutes · Primary and secondary sources, citation You need: The valley’s almanac and a screen or printed copies. Find the almanac entry nearest to today’s date, or a student’s birthday. Open the county history page it cites. Read the whole paragraph around the date. Decide: was the writer there? How many years after the event did they write? Who told them? Write a one-sentence citation for the source, with book, year and page. Going further: Look for the same event in a newspaper of the time and compare the two accounts. Weighing the evidence Grades 6 to 12 · 50 minutes · Evaluating sources, reasoning from evidence You need: Reading gravestones and the death certificate guide and a screen or printed copies. Read the guide together. List who made a gravestone, a death certificate and a county history, and when. Give pairs a disagreement: an age on a stone and an age on a certificate that differ by a year. Each pair decides which to trust and writes why, using the guide’s questions. Share: what extra record would settle it? Going further: Play one of the open cases on the case board as a class, and post the class’s answer. Notes for teachers Every source is public domain and credited where it is held. Students can open the original every time. The junior hunt , seven questions answered from the maps and directories, makes a good warm-up: Junior surveyors . Nothing to dig, nowhere to trespass. Every answer is in a book, a map or a record. Please teach the same rule on any field trip. Ideas, corrections, or a class that solved a case? Write to research@projectscroll.com . t: Document of the month
x: ← Project Scroll Document of the month · October 2026 One page of Rogers, 1875 Every month we put one real page on the table and read it slowly. This month: page 253 of Howard S. Rogers’s History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 , the first time the joke lodge of 1846 was ever printed, with the man who told it to Rogers only a footnote away. Rogers, 1875, p. 253. The boxed paragraphs are the lodge story. Tap or click the page to see it full size. What it is Rogers was Cass County’s first historian. His book came out in 1875, fifty years after the county’s first land entries, while people who had seen 1846 were still alive to be asked. That is the book’s value and its danger at once: it is close to the events, and it is made of what people remembered. How to read it Read past the quotation. Rogers quotes a long passage and then adds a few words of his own. The words after the closing quotation mark are where a careful reader slows down. Watch the punctuation. On the next page a single question mark sits inside a parenthesis. A question mark in a county history is a historian telling you, as plainly as he dared, that he is not sure. Find the teller. The passage is a quotation, and Rogers was not there in 1846. Seven years later Alfred Mathews reprinted the passage and put the teller’s name in a footnote: James M. Shepard, who was three years old in 1846. Who told him? Count what can be counted. Two hundred badges, one ball, one winter. Each number is a thing that might have left a record somewhere else: a newspaper, a bill, a diary, a badge in a drawer. Read it yourself The whole book is free online in the University of Michigan’s county-histories collection: Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 . Go to pages 253–254. Then compare Mathews, 1882 , page 174, where the same story is printed again, and notice what is missing. This page is the opening clue of Case 1 . If you read it closely enough, you may not need the rest. Next month This is the first document of the month. The next is chosen on the first of November. t: Dowagiac, Michigan history and records
x: ← The places Cass County, Michigan Dowagiac, Michigan: its history, in the record Dowagiac grew where the Michigan Central Railroad crossed Dowagiac Creek in 1848, and was incorporated as a village in 1863 and a city in 1877. Its name is Potawatomi, from a word usually read as “fishing water.” It became the county’s manufacturing town: the Round Oak Stove works, founded by P. D. Beckwith in 1871, and the grain drills of the Dowagiac Manufacturing Company. The town at a glance Founded: settled at the railroad crossing, 1848; village 1863; city 1877. Name: Potawatomi, for the creek; several spellings in the early record. In the county histories: Rogers (1875), Mathews (1882) and Glover (1906) each give the village its own chapter, with the first merchants, mills and churches named. On the map: the 1860 wall map carries a plan of Dowagiac with its lots; lay it over today’s streets . Industry: Round Oak stoves from 1871; at its height in the 1910s the works employed about 1,200 of the town’s 5,000 people. On old postcards Beckwith Building, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912, C. R. Childs Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source M.C. R.R. Station, Dowagiac, Mich · 1910, Will P. Canaan Co. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source M. C. Railway and Drill Works, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source Our New Fire Truck, Homecoming Aug. 1912, Dowagiac, Mich · 1912 Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan · source From public-domain postcards and photographs, each linked to the library that holds it. See them all . Where to look Dowagiac’s records are thick: a weekly press from the 1860s and a daily later, the Round Oak company papers, and city directories from the 1890s that list the heads of every household. The desk reads them for Cass County families as a matter of course. The records page links each source where it is held, and the glossary explains the words the old records use. t: The County Seats Loop
x: ← History drives A history drive · about 142 miles · about 3 hr 20 min of driving The County Seats Loop Every county in the valley fought over where its courthouse would stand, because the county seat brought the courts, the lawyers, the land office trade and the newspaper. Cassopolis was chosen in 1831 as a compromise between rival settlements; Centreville was named the seat of St. Joseph County the same year; Paw Paw won Van Buren County in 1837 and held it in a vote of 1901; and Berrien County moved its seat from Berrien Springs to St. Joseph by fewer than twenty votes in 1894. This loop visits four county seats and the old seat at Berrien Springs, where Michigan's oldest surviving courthouse still stands, and comes home through Niles, the river city that lost the contest. Most of these are working government buildings: look from the square, read the markers, and go inside only during office hours. Open the whole drive in Google Maps Start at stop 1 The map opens here. The numbers follow the stops below. The dashed line joins the stops in order; it is not the road route. About 142 miles and 3 hours 20 minutes of driving as a full loop, not counting stops (road distances from OpenStreetMap routing). It splits easily into an eastern half (Cassopolis, Centreville, Paw Paw) and a western half (St. Joseph, Berrien Springs, Niles). The stops 1 Cass County Courthouse, Cassopolis 120 N. Broadway St., Cassopolis, MI 49031 The present courthouse, completed in 1899 as a wood frame with a limestone veneer, is the county's third (state marker L487, 1977): the first, of 1835, stood off the public square, and the second, a frame building of 1841, stood on it for more than half a century. That second courthouse was sold and moved to State Street, became the Colonial Opera House and later the Gem Theatre, and was torn down in 1968. The 1899 building reopened in October 2024 after renovation, as the home of county offices; the State Bar's 'Freedom Road' marker stands on its south side. Open: Markers outdoors any time; building open county office hours. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 2 St. Joseph County Courthouse, Centreville 125 W. Main St., Centreville, MI 49032 Territorial Governor George B. Porter named Centreville the seat in 1831, and landowners gave the county the public square and 56 lots that November. The Greek Revival courthouse of 1842 came down in 1899, and this red brick and sandstone Romanesque Revival building by Sidney J. Osgood of Grand Rapids was dedicated on 1 August 1900, with a clock bought by the village (state marker L1150A; National Register, 1993). A courts building added on the south side of the square in the 1970s is joined to it by a glass passage. Open: Exterior and marker any time; county offices keep weekday hours. (The district court is housed in the old courthouse during the courts building's renovation, from April 2026.) Directions to this stop Source 3 Van Buren County Courthouse, Paw Paw 212 E. Paw Paw St., Paw Paw, MI 49079 The Board of Supervisors chose Paw Paw as the county seat in 1837, and a county-seat fight ended with a vote of 1901 that kept it here (state marker 556, 1990). The cornerstone of this Classical Revival courthouse, with its Italian Renaissance clock tower, was laid on 2 September 1901 and the building dedicated on 23 February 1903; Claire Allen of Jackson was the architect. It is on the National Register (1979) and still serves as the county's courthouse. Open: Marker on East Paw Paw Street any time; building open county office hours. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 4 Paw Paw City Hall, the 1840s courthouse 111 E. Michigan Ave., Paw Paw, MI 49079 Two blocks away stands the county's first courthouse, begun in 1842 and occupied in 1845: a two-story Greek Revival temple front with six columns and a Palladian window. When the county decided in 1900 to build anew, it was moved off the courthouse lot to this corner, and it serves as Paw Paw's

t: The Freedom Road
x: ← History drives A history drive · about 83 miles · about 2 hr of driving The Freedom Road In August 1847 a party of Kentuckians came to the Quaker farms of Young's Prairie to carry nine people back into slavery. Their neighbors stopped them near O'Dell's mill, where Vandalia stands now, walked raiders and captives together to Cassopolis, and a commissioner there set the nine free. That same day a party of fifty-two freedom seekers started north for Canada, fed on the way by Dr. Nathan Thomas and his wife at Schoolcraft. This drive follows the story in that order: the free Black farming community of Calvin Township, the markers at Vandalia, the Bonine House, the Bogue boulder, the courthouse square at Cassopolis, and then the road north to Schoolcraft and Battle Creek, where Erastus Hussey kept his station and Sojourner Truth made her home. Every stop is a public place or is seen from the public road; please respect private land and posted hours. Open the whole drive in Google Maps Start at stop 1 The map opens here. The numbers follow the stops below. The dashed line joins the stops in order; it is not the road route. About 83 miles and 2 hours of driving, not counting stops (road distances from OpenStreetMap routing). The run from Cassopolis to Schoolcraft goes back east along M-60 through Vandalia. The stops 1 Chain Lake Baptist Church (view from the road) Chain Lake Street, 0.6 mile east of Carver Road, Calvin Township, Cass County, MI (the marker's nearest address, per HMdb: 16853 Chain Lake St., Cassopolis, MI 49031) A state historical marker (L1352, 1992) stands on Chain Lake Street at the site of the first African American church in Cass County, organized in 1838 by the marker's account; the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County dates the congregation's incorporation to 4 January 1848, with a frame church built in 1860. The marker tells how free Black families settled for good in Calvin Township alongside the Quaker farms. It is a working church on a quiet road: read the marker from the roadside and do not walk the grounds. Open: View from the road; marker readable any time. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 2 Milo E. Barnes Park markers, Vandalia State Street (M-60) at Water Street, Vandalia, MI 49095 Two markers stand a few steps apart in the village where O'Dell's mill stood: the state's 'Underground Railroad' marker (S137) of 1957, which calls Vandalia the junction of two Underground Railroad routes, and the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County's 'Kentucky Raid' marker. Near here, Rogers wrote in 1875, the raiders were surrounded by neighbors 'armed with rifles, shot-guns, straw cutters, axes, clubs.' The park is Stop 1 of the society's own Underground Railroad driving tour. Open: Public park; markers readable any time. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 3 James E. Bonine House and carriage house 18970 M-60, Vandalia, MI 49095 (M-60 at Penn Road) A brick house with a mansard tower and, across M-60, a small Gothic carriage house, owned since December 2010 by the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County. James E. Bonine married Sarah Ann Bogue, daughter of Stephen Bogue, whose farm the raiders struck; his farm was famous for an elk park, and the 1882 county history says elk from it were sold to the King of Italy. The tower came with a remodeling after the Civil War, and the story that freedom seekers sheltered in the carriage house is the society's tradition, not yet found in a written record. t: The Fruit Belt
x: ← History drives A history drive · about 46 miles · about 1 hr 15 min of driving The Fruit Belt Lake Michigan tempers the weather along a narrow strip of shore, and by the 1840s Berrien County was already shipping peaches across the lake to Chicago. Apples, cherries, berries, grapes, pears and plums followed, and the market that opened at Benton Harbor in 1860 grew into what was called, in the 1940s, the largest cash-to-growers outlet in the world. 'No tour through Michigan is complete without a ride through the famous Fruit Belt,' a motorists' guide said in 1914. This drive starts in Benton Harbor at the oldest house in town and the market itself, climbs inland to the orchards around Coloma and the growers' cooperative at Watervliet, and ends among the fruit farms and the old county seat at Berrien Springs. Go in season: farm markets and u-pick fields follow the weather, so call ahead. Open the whole drive in Google Maps Start at stop 1 The map opens here. The numbers follow the stops below. The dashed line joins the stops in order; it is not the road route. About 46 miles and 1 hour 15 minutes of driving, not counting stops (road distances from OpenStreetMap routing). Peaches run from mid-July; apples from mid-August through October; blossom time is late April to early May. The stops 1 Morton House Museum, Benton Harbor 501 Territorial Road, Benton Harbor, MI 49022 The oldest building in Benton Harbor, built in 1849 by the pioneer Eleazar Morton and his son Henry, one of the city's founders; four generations of Mortons lived here until 1936 (state marker L0037). J. Stanley Morton, Henry's son, was president of the Graham and Morton Transportation Company, whose steamboats ran between Benton Harbor and Chicago, and he added the pillars in 1912. It is now a museum of Benton Harbor history, including the city's African American community. Open: Call ahead for hours: 269-313-2106. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 2 Benton Harbor Fruit Market and 'The Fruit Belt' marker 1891 Territorial Road, Benton Harbor, MI 49022 (marker on Territorial Road at the market) The market was established in 1860 as the outlet for the region's fruit; it began downtown and moved to this Territorial Road site in 1967 with urban-renewal funds, and in season nearly 100 commodities still pass through it. The state marker 'The Fruit Belt' (S0155, 1958) stands on Territorial Road and tells how the lake's influence made the coast a fruit country and Benton Harbor 'one of the world's major fruit markets.' It is a working wholesale market for growers and buyers: watch from the public road and keep clear of trucks. Open: Marker any time. The market trades seasonally from summer, as produce arrives; it is wholesale, not a retail stand. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 3 Jollay Orchards, Coloma 1850 Friday Road, Coloma, MI 49038 The same family has farmed this land since 1857; the orchard counts the 2026 harvest as its 170th and its owners as the eighth generation. Cherries, blueberries and peaches are picked in summer, apples and grapes in fall, and the farm market sells fresh apple cider, apple-cinnamon doughnuts and caramel apples. It is one of the three stops on Project Scroll's harvest passport trail. Open: Seasonal, June through November; hours and admission on the farm's Summer Hours page or by phone, 269-468-3075. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 4 Fruit Acres Farm Market & U-Pick, Coloma U-pick: 2789 Friday Road, Coloma, MI 49038 (farm market: 3452 Friday Road) A mile up Friday Road, a second family fruit farm with u-pick sweet and tart cherries, peaches and apples, and pumpkins in fall. t: The Makers' Road
x: ← History drives A history drive · about 64 miles · about 2 hr of driving The Makers' Road For a century the towns along the St. Joseph River made things the whole country knew by name: Round Oak stoves and Heddon lures at Dowagiac, Kawneer storefronts at Niles, Studebaker wagons and cars and Oliver plows at South Bend, Ball-Band boots at Mishawaka, Conn band horns and, later, recreational vehicles at Elkhart. This drive runs downriver and then east along it, from the stove town to Goshen, stopping at the museums that keep the makers' work and the markers that stand where the factories did. Most of the great works are gone; where something survives, it is noted, and where it is a working plant or private property, you look from the road. Open the whole drive in Google Maps Start at stop 1 The map opens here. The numbers follow the stops below. The dashed line joins the stops in order; it is not the road route. About 64 miles and 2 hours of driving, not counting stops (road distances from OpenStreetMap routing). The South Bend museums and the Elkhart hall of fame each deserve an hour or more; Indiana and Michigan stops on this drive are all on Eastern time. The stops 1 Dowagiac Area History Museum 201 E. Division St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 The stove town's museum, free, with the story of the Round Oak Stove Company: Philo D. Beckwith cast his first stove around 1867 to heat his struggling foundry, and by 1900 Round Oak was one of the largest stove factories in the United States, with about 1,200 workers in the 1910s. The museum also keeps grain-drill artifacts from Beckwith's earlier drill trade. The 1910s Round Oak foundry complex on Spaulding Street still stands and is in industrial use; see it from the street only. Open: Tuesday to Friday 10 to 5, Saturday 10 to 2. Free. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 2 Heddon Museum 115 S. Front St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 James Heddon, a former beekeeper, is said to have got the idea for a top-water lure by Dowagiac's Mill Pond in the late 1890s; the company was founded in 1902, began in the family kitchen, and was making lures in a Dowagiac factory by 1904, most of its workers women. Lures were made here until 1984. The museum holds more than 1,000 lures, 140 reels and 150 rods, including an original James Heddon frog. Open: Tuesday and Friday 10 to 5; run by volunteers, so call ahead: 269-783-2560. Directions to this stop More on Project Scroll › Source 3 Plym Park, Niles 401 Marmont St., Niles, MI 49120 Francis J. Plym, a Swedish-born architect, patented a copper frame for plate-glass shop windows in 1906 and moved his Kawneer Company to Niles in early 1907; it grew from window frames to door frames and complete storefronts. t: Elkhart, Indiana: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Elkhart County, Indiana Elkhart Elkhart stands where the Elkhart River runs into the St. Joseph. Dr. Havilah Beardsley laid out the town in 1832 on the point between the two rivers, beside an older settlement and post office called Pulaski. It became a town in 1858 and a city in 1875, and a hydraulic canal built around 1870 turned the river into factory power. In 1874 Charles G. Conn began making cornet mouthpieces here, and Elkhart became the nation's band-instrument town. At a glance Founded platted by Havilah Beardsley, 1832; town, 1858; city, 1875 Name Chapman's county history (1881) says Beardsley named the town Elkhart because the island at the meeting of the rivers was shaped so much like an elk's heart, and that the Pulaski post office later took the name. Scholars trace the name further back, to an elk's-heart place name recorded in French in the 1700s Water power "The hydraulic works of 1870 opened up a new era in the progress of the town," Chapman wrote in 1881; mills and factories lined the canal Band instruments C. G. Conn began making cornet mouthpieces in 1874, then brass instruments; Conn, Buescher, Selmer and others made Elkhart a national center of the trade Medicine Franklin Miles founded the Miles Medical Company here in 1884; it later made Alka-Seltzer County seat no; Goshen, ten miles up the Elkhart River, is the county seat of Elkhart County Worth a visit Ruthmere (Albert R. Beardsley House) , 302 E. Beardsley Ave., Elkhart. The Beardsley family mansion on the river, now a house museum with a fine-arts collection. National Register, 1978. Dr. Havilah Beardsley House , 102 W. Beardsley Ave., Elkhart. The house of the founder's family, on the Ruthmere grounds and open with the museum. National Register, 2000. Lerner Theatre , 401 S. Main St., Elkhart. The downtown theater, still a working stage. National Register, 1980. Elkhart Downtown Commercial Historic District , Main St., roughly between E. Jackson St. and Tyler Ave., Elkhart. The brick business blocks along Main Street. National Register, 1997. Where the records are Deeds, probate and marriage records are kept by Elkhart County at Goshen, the county seat. The Elkhart Public Library keeps its local history collection on the second floor of the downtown library, with city directories, a searchable obituary index, a photo archive shared with Indiana Memory, and the Elkhart Truth archive. The Elkhart County Historical Museum, 304 W. Vistula St., Bristol, has a research library of photographs, diaries, family records and plat maps (appointments recommended). Chapman's History of Elkhart County (1881) and Deahl's Twentieth Century History (1905) both give the city long chapters. Sources History of Elkhart County, Indiana (Chicago: Chas. C. t: Family histories and registers
x: ← Research services Research services Family histories, built to be checked Most family trees are copied from other family trees. Ours are built from the records themselves: every name, date and place marked with where it came from, every gap shown honestly, and every family story kept exactly as it was told, beside the evidence that tests it. What we make Looking down A family register Every descendant of one couple, generation by generation, each person given a number, so that a reader can follow any branch from the first settlers to the present day. The form genealogists have trusted for 150 years. Looking back An ancestral monograph Your ancestors, back as far as the records honestly go, on a single chart. Where a line stops, it says whose parents are wanting, so you can see at a glance what is known, what is not, and where to look next. The whole story A family history Every line written up as a story, with the evidence beneath it: maps, records, a list of every source, an index of names and places, and the open questions set out for the next person to take up. A specimen monograph Here is how an ancestral monograph works, using an invented family. Tap anyone to see what we know about them, and how we know it. Specimen. The names are invented; the method is real. Tap a name in the chart. “Clara ?” A question mark means the marriage is recorded but her own surname is not. Women are usually recorded under their husbands’ names, which is not the same as being born with them. “Wanting” An empty box beside a known person is a real gap: someone we could find tomorrow. The boxes beyond the edge of the chart, behind Clara’s missing parents, are not gaps at all. There is nothing to look for there until her parents are found. The warning sign. When two records cannot both be true, the chart flags the joint and leaves it in. Never solve a problem by deleting the evidence. How a register reads 1. AUGUST¹ BRANDT was born about 1862 Inference and died in 1931 Document . He married WILHELMINA KRAUSE , born in 1866 Document . Children of August and Wilhelmina: + 2 i. OTTO² , born 1890; married CLARA ? ii. Emma, born 1893; died 1894, aged one. The small raised number is the generation. The plus sign means Otto’s own family is carried forward under his number, 2, so a reader can follow his line on down without losing the thread. (The same invented family as the chart above.) Lessons from our own desk Every one learned the hard way, on a family history built at this desk. A woman dies under her married name. For years a death certificate went unfound because everyone searched for her under her maiden name. It was filed under her husband’s. Search the unusual name. A rare surname finds the family and almost nobody else. A common one needs a place and a date beside it, or it finds thousands. A strong lead in the right county is still not a parent. A well-documented man of the right name, in the right place, at the right time, turned out to be no relation at all. The answer was in a different family. An abstract is not a record. A published summary of a colonial will gave two witnesses’ names and a probate date. The court’s own record disagreed on both. “About” must stay “about.” A birth year worked out from an age at death was printed beside real dates, and soon looked like one. Estimates are marked as estimates, always. The best finds are in free books nobody opened. Lines written off as dead ends turned out to be answered in county histories and family genealogies that had been free online for years. Dead ends don’t get searched. Starting your family’s history Tell us who. One couple to work down from, or one person to work back from. Names, places, rough dates. Send what the family has. Bible pages, letters, photographs, obituaries, old trees. We read every one, and we keep every family story exactly as it was told. Agree on the shape. A register, a monograph, a full history, or a single line to begin with. We build it from the records. Ce

t: Questions people ask
x: ← Project Scroll Questions people ask Search the questions No question matches that yet. Email us or ask on Facebook . Does the hunt cost anything? No. The hunt is free to follow and free to play. All you need is curiosity and, now and then, a library card. Do I have to go anywhere? No. Every clue is solved on paper: in books, maps and records, many of them free online. The hunt never sends anyone onto private land or near a grave. I solved one. Now what? Post your answer in the comments on Facebook , with the book and page, or the link, where you found it. The first solver who can show the page is named in the next post and on the case board, and gets a solver’s keepsake to print. I’ve never done research before. Can I play? Yes. Every case page has a “Start here” box with the first pages to open, many of them free online. The glossary explains the old words, the guides show you how to read a death certificate and old handwriting , and the hunter’s worksheet keeps your notes straight. All you need is curiosity and, now and then, a library card. Can you help with my own family’s mystery? Yes. Write to research@projectscroll.com , or send Project Scroll a message on Facebook, with what you know. We’ll tell you honestly what the records are likely to show before you commit to anything. Can you write up my whole family’s history? Yes. We make family registers (every descendant of one couple), ancestral monographs (every ancestor of one person) and full family histories, built from the records with every statement marked. See a specimen , or download the sample family register . Do you also offer imaging, design, photography, 3D or video? Yes. Alongside the research, we scan and restore old photographs and documents, bring up faded ink, design family-history books and charts, design and build websites, photograph heirlooms and places, model landscapes in 3D from public LiDAR surveys, make 3D animations and family-history films, and keep living documents that grow with the research. See the studio work , then send us a message with what you have and what you would like made. What should I keep notes on? Use the hunter’s worksheet : one page to log each record, who made it, when, and where you found it. Print as many as you need. Is anything hidden on this website? Perhaps. There is a line of code at the foot of every page, a gold diamond that answers if asked, more than thirty tin badges to earn, and every page has a back side. Curious hunters know where to look. Who runs Project Scroll? An independent researcher and author who writes narrative nonfiction about the history of the Great Lakes country, trained in visual communications. The research behind those books is the same research we offer you, and the imaging and design studio grew from that training. More about Project Scroll . How is the hunt paid for? By sponsors: friends who give a few dollars a month, patrons who fund a case, local businesses with a card in the sponsors’ strip, and organizations that underwrite a hall. Sponsorship funds the work and never shapes a finding. How it works, and the ledger of what every gift paid for . How do I get in touch? Email research@projectscroll.com , or message the page on Facebook . Both reach the same desk. The form below lays out what to include. Expect a first reply within a few days; a full read of your records takes longer, and we say how long before we start. How long does a research case take? It depends on the question and on what survives. Some mysteries open in an afternoon; some take a season. After the first read we tell you what we expect to find, and roughly how long it should take, before you commit to anything. Does this website track me? Only if you say yes. On your first visit the site asks whether it may count your visit with a small Meta script; until you choose Allow, nothing is loaded and nothing is counted, and you can change your answer on the Privacy page. t: Getting here: by car, air, train and bus
x: ← Visit & Plan Planes, trains and the open road Getting here Cassopolis sits in the middle of the St. Joseph River valley, an easy drive from Chicago, Detroit, Indianapolis and Grand Rapids, with an airport at South Bend and Amtrak stations at Dowagiac and Niles, two of the valley’s handsomest old depots. Allow extra time around Chicago, where the clock is also an hour behind. By air South Bend International Airport (SBN) , about 27 miles, 43 min by car to Cassopolis. The closest airport; the South Shore Line train to Chicago leaves from the airport station. Airport site Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) , about 135 miles, 3 h 13 min by car to Cassopolis. Airport site By train Niles Amtrak station (NLS): Wolverine (Chicago–Detroit–Pontiac, three daily round trips) and Blue Water (Chicago–Port Huron, one daily round trip). Station building with waiting room, parking, accessible platform. The Michigan Central built the depot in 1892 (Spier and Rohns, architects); its tower and gardens are a local landmark. History source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niles_station_(Michigan) Station page Dowagiac Amtrak station (DOA): Wolverine and Blue Water. The nearest station to Cassopolis. Not on the Michigan Wolverine/Blue Water line. Station page South Shore Line (commuter rail to Chicago) : Electric commuter trains between South Bend Airport and Millennium Station in downtown Chicago, with stops including Hudson Lake and Michigan City. A future relocation of the South Bend station is planned but no date is set; check service notices (in October 2026 some Chicago stops were bus-substituted). t: The glossary
x: ← Project Scroll From the desk The glossary The words old records use, and the words we use about them, in plain English. Learn a handful, and an old deed or gravestone starts to talk. Find a word Abstract A summary of a document, such as a deed or will, giving its main points. Useful for finding the original, but not the record itself: abstracts drop words and sometimes get names and dates wrong. Administrator The person a court appoints to settle the estate of someone who died without a will. Compare executor. Ahnentafel German for “ancestor table.” A numbering system for a pedigree: the subject is 1, a person’s father is double their number and their mother double plus one. So 2 is the father, 3 the mother, 4 the father’s father. Census A count of the population. The United States has taken one every ten years since 1790; from 1850 it names every free person in the household (enslaved people were counted on separate schedules, usually without names, until 1870). Most of the 1890 census was destroyed after a fire in 1921. Each census is opened to the public 72 years after it was taken. Consort A husband or wife. Often seen on old gravestones: “Mary, consort of John Smith.” County history The big county histories printed from the 1870s to the 1910s. Many biographies in them were paid for by the people they describe, so they tend to be reliable on what the family knew well, and generous on everything else; dates and places still need a document. Deed The written record of land changing hands, copied into the county’s deed books. Deeds often name wives, heirs and neighbors, and sometimes say where a seller had moved to. Ditto (do.) “The same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it, or a pair of marks, for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. Double dating Dates such as “10 February 1731/2.” Before 1752, England and its colonies began the new year on 25 March, so January to March dates were often written with both years. Et ux. Latin, “and wife,” in deeds and court records: “John Smith et ux.” means John and his wife. Executor The person named in a will to carry it out. Compare administrator. Field notes A surveyor’s notebook from the original land survey, recording every line walked: the trees, streams, soil and sometimes the people met along the way. General Land Office The federal office that surveyed and sold public land, from 1812 until it became part of the Bureau of Land Management in 1946. Its plats, field notes and patents are free online. Informant The person who answered the questions on a certificate. On a death certificate the dead person was never the informant, so everything on it is someone else’s memory. Instant and ultimo Old newspaper shorthand: “the 4th inst.” means the 4th of this month; “the 20th ult.” the 20th of last month. Intestate Having died without a will. The court then appoints an administrator and divides the estate by law. Land patent The first transfer of a piece of land from the government to a private owner. Local legend The famous ancestor, the buried treasure, the river under the ground. Some are true. The desk reads each one against the record and says which. Long s (ſ) An s that looks like an f without the full crossbar, used at the start or in the middle of a word until about 1800. “Congreſs” is Congress. Lore What a place says about itself: the stories passed around a lake, a township or a lodge, told without a page to point to. Lore is where a hunt often starts; the record is where it ends. Maiden name A woman’s surname before marriage. Most records name married women only by their husbands’ surnames, which is why a woman’s own family is the commonest gap in any tree. mtDNA and Y-DNA Two DNA tests that follow one line each: mitochondrial DNA passes from mother to child down the all-female line; Y-DNA passes from father to son down the all-male line. t: Goshen, Indiana: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Elkhart County, Indiana Goshen Goshen was made to be a county seat. In 1831 the Elkhart County commissioners chose the high ground on the Elkhart River as the most suitable point, ordered their agent Oliver Crane to lay out a town, and sold the first lots that July. It was incorporated as a town in 1854 and as a city in 1868. That same year a hydraulic canal, dug to carry the river's water past the mills, was finished, and Goshen became a mill and factory town around its courthouse square. At a glance Founded laid out as the county seat, 1831; first lots sold July 1831; town, 1854; city, 1868 Name Chapman's county history (1881) says Oliver Crane, who came from near Goshen, New York, gave the town its name; the Goshen Historical Society points to the Biblical Land of Goshen, a name for fertile ground County seat yes, of Elkhart County since 1831; the courthouse stands on the square downtown Water power the hydraulic canal, begun about 1866 and completed in 1868, drew water from the Elkhart River to run flour mills and factories, as Chapman described in 1881 A college Goshen College, a Mennonite college, dates from 1894 Worth a visit Elkhart County Courthouse , Courthouse Square, Goshen. The county courthouse on the square, the center of Goshen since its founding as the county seat. National Register, 1980. Goshen Historic District , Downtown Goshen, between Pike St., Main St., Purl St. and the canal. The downtown and the old residential streets around it, bounded in part by the hydraulic canal. National Register, 1983. Goshen Carnegie Public Library , 202 N. 5th St., Goshen. The town's Carnegie library building. National Register, 1983. Goshen Historical Society museum , 124 S. Main St., Goshen. Exhibits on the city's history, open Tuesday through Saturday. Where the records are Goshen is the county seat, so Elkhart County's deeds, probate, marriage and court records are kept here. The Goshen Public Library's Indiana Room has Goshen newspapers on microfilm from 1837 to 2022, Goshen city directories from 1883 (selected years), an obituary card file from 1970 and a Goshen News index from 2007. The Goshen Historical Society runs a museum at 124 S. Main St. The Elkhart County Historical Museum, 304 W. Vistula St., Bristol, has a research library with plat maps and family records. Chapman's 1881 county history gives the city of Goshen its own long chapter. Sources History of Elkhart County, Indiana (Chicago: Chas. C. Chapman, 1881): site chosen as "the most suitable point"; Oliver Crane "coming from the vicinity of Goshen, New York, gave name to the town" (page 393); Crane ordered to lay out the town (page 416); lots sold by Crane in July 1831 (page 884, under "CITY OF GOSHEN"); "THE HYDRAULIC CANAL" (page 905) link Goshen Historical Society, "Historical Society History" (platted 1831; town 1854; city 1868; name from the Biblical Land of Goshen; museum at 124 S. Main St.) link Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Goshen" (seat 1831; Goshen College 1894; name probably for Goshen, New York) link City of Goshen, "About" (settled 1831; county seat) link Goshen Public Library, "Genealogy & Local History" (Indiana Room holdings) link Wikipedia, "National Register of Historic Places listings in Elkhart County, Indiana" link Elkhart County Parks, "Elkhart County Historical Museum" link Dates and names are from the county histories and official sources listed here. t: How do I read a Michigan death certificate?
x: ← Project Scroll A guide from the desk How do I read a Michigan death certificate? A death certificate is two records in one. The doctor wrote down the death, at the time. Someone else, the informant, answered questions about a whole life, on the hardest day. Tap any numbered box to see who filled it in, and how far to trust it. Box 11 Informant Filled in by: How far to trust it: Every box, in order The rule of thumb The top half (boxes 3 to 10) is memory : what the informant believed about a life. The bottom half (boxes 12 to 16) is the event : written by people who were there that week. When either half disagrees with another record, trust the bottom half first, and weigh the top half by who the informant was. Remember: the dead person was never the informant. Everything in the top half is someone else’s memory, given on the hardest day, so find the informant’s name on the certificate and ask how well they knew the life they were describing. Michigan’s certificates from 1897 to 1952 are free to view at the Archives of Michigan . Elsewhere, try FamilySearch or your state archives. t: How do I read an old gravestone?
x: ← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk Reading old gravestones A gravestone is a record, cut in stone by a family that wanted to be remembered. It is also often wrong: carved years after the death, from memory, by a stonecutter paid by the letter. Here is how to read one, and how far to trust it. What the stone is telling you willow · urn Willow and urn A weeping willow over an urn: mourning, carved most often from about the 1790s to the 1850s. A rough date for a stone whose numbers have worn away. lamb A lamb Usually a child’s grave. Lambs on small stones are among the commonest carvings of the 1800s. a hand A hand pointing up Hope of heaven. A hand reaching down from a cloud is God calling the soul home; it does not mean a sudden death, though it is often read that way. two hands Clasped hands A farewell, or a marriage. Look at the cuffs: a man’s and a woman’s sleeve mean husband and wife. FLT Three linked rings The Odd Fellows, a fraternal order: Friendship, Love and Truth. A lead to a lodge’s records and its burial benefit. square · compass Square and compass The Freemasons. Like the rings, it points to a lodge that may have kept minutes and paid for the funeral. G.A.R. A bronze star or flag holder The Grand Army of the Republic, the society of Union veterans of the Civil War. The man was a soldier; look for his regiment. a shield A marble stone with a sunk shield A government headstone for a Union soldier, with his company and regiment cut in the shield: the key to his service record and pension file. ætat · æ In the 74th year of his age “Ætat.” or “æ.” means aged. “In the 74th year of his age” means he was 73: the 74th year began on his 73rd birthday. 23y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death to the birth date with the age calculator . consort · relict Wife or widow “Consort of” means his wife, who died while he lived. “Relict of” means his widow, who outlived him. marble · granite What it is made of Marble, white or grey, was usual from about the 1830s to 1900 and dissolves slowly in the rain, so its letters soften. Granite took over from the late 1800s. A hollow, blue-grey stone with crisp letters is “white bronze”, cast zinc, sold from the 1870s to about 1914. How far to trust a stone When was it carved? Many stones were put up years after the burial, and a family stone listing several people was often cut all at once, long after the first death. The dates on it are memories. Who paid for it? The family, so the stone says what the family believed: the age they remembered, the spelling they used. Check it against a record made at the time: a death certificate, a church burial register, a newspaper notice, the cemetery’s own book. Where they disagree, the record made at the time usually wins. See how to read a death certificate . A missing stone is not a missing grave. Wooden markers rotted, stones broke and were cleared away, and many people never had a stone at all. Reading a worn stone, without harming it Use raking light. Hold a mirror or a torch low and to one side so the light skims across the face; the letters appear in shadow. Try different times of day. Photograph it straight on and at an angle, with the light coming from several sides. Never use shaving cream, flour, chalk, bleach, wire brushes or household cleaners. They stay in the stone and eat it. Do not make rubbings of soft, flaking or leaning stones; on a sound stone, ask the cemetery first. Leave it as you found it. Do not lean on stones, prop them up or move pieces. Report damage to the cemetery’s keeper. Be a good visitor Keep to the paths and the cemetery’s hours, and ask permission before entering a private family plot. Never dig, probe or disturb the ground, and never take anything away. It is wrong, and in Michigan and Indiana, as elsewhere, it can be a crime. No case on Project Scroll ever needs it. Remember the families. The people buried here have descendants nearby. t: How do I read old handwriting in records?
x: ← The hunter’s toolkit A guide from the desk How do I read old handwriting in records? The writing in old records is not hard once you know ten tricks the clerks used. Here they are, with a short quiz at the end. The clerks’ tricks ſ The long s Looks like an f without the full crossbar. Used at the start or middle of a word until about 1800: “Congreſs”, “ſon”, “Miſsiſsippi”. Read it as an ordinary s. ye “Ye” means “the” The y stands for an old letter, thorn (þ), pronounced “th”. “Ye olde inn” was always read “the old inn”. Likewise “yt” = that, “ym” = them. Wm · Jno · Chas Shortened first names Clerks raised the last letters: Wm = William, Jno = John (not Jonathan), Chas = Charles, Thos = Thomas, Jas = James, Geo = George, Saml = Samuel, Benj = Benjamin. inst. · ult. · prox. Which month? “The 4th inst.” = the 4th of this month. “The 20th ult.” = the 20th of last month. “The 2nd prox.” = the 2nd of next month. Check the date of the letter or newspaper to know which month. do. Ditto “do.” under an entry means “the same as above.” Census takers and clerks used it for repeated surnames, birthplaces and occupations. &c. Et cetera The ampersand plus c: “and so on”. Often written as a looped sign that can look like a letter. 1745/6 Double dates Before 1752 in England and its colonies, the new year began on 25 March. A date between January and March is often written with both years. Use the later one for today’s calendar. relict · consort On gravestones “Relict of John Smith” = his widow (she outlived him). “Consort of” = his wife, who died while he was living. dec’d · Esq. In deeds and wills dec’d = deceased. Esq. = Esquire, a courtesy for a lawyer or a man of standing, not a title of nobility. 71y 4m 12d Ages to the day Age at death in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death with the age calculator . Test yourself Six questions. A letter dated 10 June says “your note of the 28th ult.” When was the note written? “ult.” means last month: 28 May. In a 1790 newspaper you read “Congreſs”. What does it say? That f-like letter is the long s. A census line reads “Jno Smith” and below it “do. do.” What is the second person’s name? Jno is John, and do. repeats the line above. A gravestone reads “Mary, relict of Amos Hale.” What does it tell you? A relict outlived her husband. A baptism is dated “12 February 1734/5”. Which year is it on today’s calendar? Use the later year for January to March dates before 1752. “Ye Olde Tavern” was read aloud as… The y stands for the old letter thorn, “th”. t: Heirlooms
x: ← Project Scroll Heirlooms What the valley handed down A stove from the Round Oak works. A lure carved in Dowagiac. A quilt pieced in a Porter Township farmhouse. Most of the valley’s history isn’t in a museum. It sits in a parlour, on a mantel, in a box in the attic. This is a cabinet for those things, and for the stories that came with them. The cabinet The cabinet is empty, and waiting for the first piece. Every shelf will hold something a family in the valley still keeps, shown with its owner’s yes and in their words. The kinds of thing we hope to see: A Round Oak stove, or anything cast in Dowagiac A Heddon lure, rod or tackle box A quilt, a sampler or a coverlet, with the hands that made it A family Bible with births and deaths written in A crock, a jug or a churn from a valley pottery A tool from the farm, the mill or the shop A letter, a diary, a ledger or a receipt A school medal, a band uniform, a lodge apron Add a piece Tell us about it here. The page writes an email for you. Nothing is sent until you press send. Send a photograph or two. Attach them to the email: the whole thing, and any mark, label or signature on it. Nothing goes in the cabinet without your yes. We send you exactly what would appear. You can say no, change it, or leave your name off. We never show where you live. Your heirloom What is it? t: Is the family story true?
x: ← Research services Mysteries in the family Is the family story true? Every family has a story that has been told so often nobody questions it. Some are true. Some are half-true. Some began as a guess a hundred years ago. The records can usually tell which. Test a family legend Choose the story your family tells. Pick a story above to see what the records usually say about it, and how we would test yours. Tradition What families say. An inspector couldn’t spell it, so he wrote down something easier, and that became the family name. Document What the records usually show. Ellis Island inspectors did not write names down; they checked arrivals against passenger lists made at the port of departure. Names did change, often, but usually years later and by the family itself: at naturalization, at work, at school, or simply over time. How we test it Find the passenger list: it shows the name as written where the journey began. Find the naturalization papers, which often record both the old name and the new one. Follow the name census by census to see when the new spelling first appears. Reading The change almost always happened. Ellis Island almost never did it. Tradition What families say. A lord, a king, a governor or a famous founder sits at the top of the tree. Document What the records usually show. Some of these are true. Many began as a name match: someone of the right surname, in roughly the right place, adopted into the tree a century ago and copied forward until it looked like fact. How we test it Test the line one link at a time, starting with the most recent. Every parent–child joint needs its own record. Find who first printed the claim, and what they cited. Check the famous person’s documented children against the one the family claims. Reading Worth testing. Usually the line breaks at one particular joint, and finding it is a story in itself. Tradition What families say. A grandmother or great-grandmother was a Native princess, often said to be Cherokee. Document What the records usually show. The Cherokee Nation did not have princesses, and the story is so widespread that historians treat it as a family-legend pattern of its own. Some families do have Native ancestry, and the records that show it are specific: tribal rolls, agency censuses and treaty and allotment papers. How we test it Name the ancestor and place her in a census, with the people around her. Search the tribal rolls of the place and period (for the Cherokee: the Dawes and Guion Miller rolls, and the earlier rolls before them). A DNA test cannot show tribal membership; only the records and the nation itself can. Reading The princess is almost never real. The ancestor sometimes is, and deserves to be found properly. Tradition What families say. Three brothers arrived on one ship: one went north, one went south and one went west. Document What the records usually show. It is one of the most common stories in American family lore. Sometimes there were three brothers. Often there were three men of the same surname who were not related at all, later joined together to explain why the name turns up in different places. How we test it Find each man separately in the passenger lists, censuses and land records. Look for a document that names them as brothers: a will, a deed, a probate file. For male lines, a Y-DNA test can say whether their descendants share a father at all. Reading Often half-true: the men were real; the brotherhood is the part to test. Tradition What families say. Everything was lost in the fire, so there is no point looking. Document What the records usually show. Courthouses did burn, and records were lost. But deeds were often re-recorded afterward by the owners, and copies survive in state archives, churches, newspapers, tax rolls, military files and the records of neighboring counties. How we test it Find out exactly which years and which books were lost: it is rarely everything. Look for deeds re-recorded after the fire. Go around it: st
