t: Lost towns of the valley
x: ← Project Scroll Lost towns of the valley Towns that are not there any more Every county history has a page of places that were platted, named, given a mill or a store, and then left behind. Here are ten from the valley: why they were started, and what became of them. Most died the same way. A mill town grew up where a creek could turn a wheel; then the railroad came through somewhere else, trade followed the rails, and the mill was all that was left. Others never lived at all: paper towns drawn up in the land boom of 1836 and sold, or not sold, to people back East. Adamsport and Christiana (later Adamsville) Ontwa Township, Cass County, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Two little plats faced each other across Christiana Creek: Christiana, laid out by Moses Sage, and Adamsport, laid out by Sterling Adams. The creek turned a grist mill, and a hotel followed. In 1882 the place had 133 people, a hotel, a blacksmith shop, a store and the mill. What happened. The two plats grew together under one name, Adamsville. When the railroads made new trading towns, it slipped back; by 1906 the mill was its only industry. “Both now are known by the name of Adamsville.” Rogers, 1875 The histories disagree on dates: Rogers puts Adamsport in September 1832 and Christiana in 1834; Mathews has March 1833 and May 1831. Williamsville Porter Township, Cass County, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Josiah Williams laid it out in 1848 and had a hand in its first store. William R. Merritt’s store, opened in 1854, became “the trading place for miles around.” In 1882: two stores, two blacksmiths, a grist mill and a sawmill, one physician, 88 people. What happened. It simply never grew. “Its population has never reached much beyond the hundred mark.” Glover, 1906 Rogers says it was laid out in March 1848; Glover says the plat was filed on 5 July 1849. Kessington (also called Sailor) Mason Township, Cass County, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Moses McKessick platted 19 lots on the Chicago road in 1872. In 1882 it had his general store, a blacksmith shop, a United Brethren church, a few houses and a schoolhouse. What happened. By 1906 the store and the smithy were gone. “one might drive over this site and notice nothing more remarkable at this country crossroads than a church and a school” Glover, 1906 Laid out 12 April 1872 (Rogers); the plat was recorded on 22 July (Mathews) or 23 July (Glover). Wakelee where four Cass County townships meet, Michigan · on today’s map What was there. Levi Garwood laid it out in 1871 on the new Peninsular railroad, later the Grand Trunk, and it was named for the line’s first treasurer, C. Wakelee. In 1882 it had 150 people, a store, a hotel, a blacksmith and a steam sawmill. What happened. It was a lumber station. When the timber was cut, the reason for it went too; it never incorporated, and its post office is long closed. “a large amount of lumber and wood is shipped from this point.” Mathews, 1882 Venice (a paper town) Wayne Township, Cass County, Michigan What was there. x: ← The map room Cassopolis in LiDAR The county seat, laser by laser In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot below is one of those echoes: 775,557 of them in the blocks around the courthouse, every one the survey kept, and 759,226 more across the country around. Around them lies the land the same survey measured, from Stone Lake to Diamond Lake, about six kilometres across. Turn it, tilt it, and lay the 1860 town plan over the real ground. Sun off Loading the survey… Drag to turn · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two fingers to move · tap the ground for a reading Buildings, 193,991 points Trees, 1,340,792 points The bare ground, with a contour every two metres Stone Lake and Diamond Lake What you are looking at Real survey points, not a drawing. Each dot is a laser return recorded by the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2015 flight over Cass County, placed to within a few centimetres. Roof shapes, chimneys and the crowns of single trees are all there because the laser hit them. The ground. The survey marks which returns struck bare earth. Those make the surface underneath, a model of the land with the buildings and trees taken off. It rises about 14 metres across these blocks. Buildings and trees. The survey does not say which of the other points are roofs and which are leaves, so we sorted them: a laser pulse that hits a roof comes back once; one that hits a tree comes back several times, from leaves, branches and the ground below. Flat, single echoes in a patch the size of a building are coloured gold. A few porches and dense evergreens may be the wrong colour. The lakes and the land around. Stone Lake lies just west of the courthouse, and Diamond Lake, with Grand Island in it, a short way east. The wider ground comes from the same 2015 flight, as the survey’s bare-earth elevation: the shape of the land every six metres or so, and its light and shade from a grid one and a half metres apart, sharp enough to show field edges, ditches and old roadbeds. The lakes are drawn flat at their surface, because the survey does not see through water. Buildings and trees are shown only in the town blocks, where every point is kept. The 1860 plan. Press 1860 plan to lay the town plan from the 1860 county wall map on the ground. Its west part reaches into these blocks. Compare it with the flat then-and-now page . The 1909 fire map. Press 1909 fire map to lay the Sanborn fire-insurance map of January 1909 on the ground: every building downtown, in pink for brick and yellow for wood, from the courthouse to the hotel. We fitted its two sheets to today’s street corners; they line up to within about a metre. Lake depths. Press Lake depths to see the bottom of Diamond Lake drawn in lines every ten feet, from the state’s lake survey. The deepest point is 64 feet, east of the island. Story pins. The gold pins are the stops of our walking tour of Cassopolis , from the site of the first courthouse to the bank corner, and the island in Diamond Lake. Press one for a line of its history. Guided tour. Press Guided tour and the view flies itself from Stone Lake to the courthouse square and out to Diamond Lake. Touch the model to stop it. Sun and shadows. Move the Sun slider through a midsummer day, from six in the morning to eight at night, and every roof and tree in the town blocks casts its shadow on the ground. The shadows are worked out from the laser points themselves. Tap for a reading. Tap or click the bare ground anywhere, and the model tells you how high it stands above sea level and how far it is from the courthouse. Buildings and Trees. Each button hides or shows its points, so you can see the bare land under the town, or the trees alone. Height ×3. The town is fairly level, so tripling the heights makes the rise of the land easier to see. The buildings stretch too. Your own place in 3D. t: The St. Joseph River Valley in 3D
x: ← The map room The valley in 3D The St. Joseph River Valley All 12,209 square kilometres that drain to the St. Joseph River, from the hills past Hillsdale to Lake Michigan, built from the U.S. Geological Survey’s laser-made elevation of the ground. The river and its branches are drawn in gold. 10 lost towns are hidden in the hills: find all 10. Height ×15 Loading the valley… Drag to turn · scroll or pinch to zoom · tap a gold light or a pin What you are looking at The whole watershed. The bright land is every acre whose rain ends in the St. Joseph River: parts of fifteen counties in Michigan and Indiana. The darker land around it drains elsewhere: to the Kalamazoo, the Maumee, the Kankakee, or straight to Lake Michigan. The shape of the ground. The heights come from the U.S. Geological Survey’s 3D Elevation Program, which in this country is made mostly from laser surveys flown county by county. Here the shape of the land is drawn every 200 metres or so, and its light and shade from a grid about 50 metres apart, sharp enough to show the river’s own bluffs and old channels. The heights are raised (×15 to start) because the valley falls only about 200 metres from its eastern hills to the lake. Use the slider to flatten it or raise it further. What the ice left. The long ridges and knobby hills are moraines, left where the glaciers stood and melted, about 15,000 years ago. The flat, open plains between them are outwash, sand and gravel spread by the meltwater. The river wanders through them both. Story pins. The gold pins mark where our stories happened, from the Dewey Lake week of 1964 to how Kalamazoo got its name. Press one for the stories told there. What the ice left. Press it to name the big landforms: the Kalamazoo moraine, which runs through Cassopolis on its way to Kalamazoo and Hastings; the Sturgis moraine, Michigan’s oldest; the Valparaiso moraine along the lake shore; and the flat outwash plains spread by the meltwater. The labels are placed by eye from published maps, near the ground they name, not on a surveyed line. Railroads. Press it to see the valley’s railroads: the lines still running in pale grey, and in rust the ones that are gone, abandoned or pulled up, many of them now trails. Fly to Cassopolis. The button flies you down into the county seat and opens Cassopolis in LiDAR , where every laser point is shown. The gold lights. Each is the site of a lost town from the county histories. Tap each one. Where only the township or the neighbourhood is known, the light stands near it and its card says “about here.” Find all 10 and the valley is yours: there is a badge for it. Your own place in 3D. Project Scroll makes LiDAR models like this one for other places: a farm, a lake, a town, an old mill site, a family’s home ground, from the same public surveys, with fly-throughs and still pictures to keep. See the studio , or write to research@projectscroll.com. The river’s fall The St. Joseph River falls about 158 metres (518 feet) on its way to Lake Michigan, most steeply in its first fifty kilometres below Hillsdale. The small blue bars are the dams on the main river today, from the Sturgis Dam near Centreville down to Berrien Springs. Heights are read from the same elevation model, along a simplified line of the river; the river’s own course, with every bend, is longer. Railroads and dams: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). t: Mishawaka, Indiana: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan St. Joseph County, Indiana Mishawaka Mishawaka began with bog iron. In 1832 Alanson Hurd sent a prospector up the St. Joseph River to look for ore, and in 1833 he bought land at the rapids and built the St. Joseph Iron Works, the town's first name. By 1837 four little towns stood side by side, and in February 1838 the legislature joined them under one name, Mishawaka. The town became a city in 1899, and its mills made Dodge pulleys, Ball-Band rubber boots and the Simplex motor car. At a glance Founded iron works and town platted, 1833; incorporated as the village of St. Joseph Iron Works, 1835; four towns united as Mishawaka by act of the legislature, February 17, 1838; city, 1899 Name from the Potawatomi; Howard's 1907 county history notes that the name Mishawaka was in use while the town's official name was still St. Joseph Iron Works, and that William Barbee's plat was the first to carry it on record. The linguist Michael McCafferty reads it as a Potawatomi word meaning "at the firewood-tree land"; the older reading, "swift water" or "big rapids," is the one the city and museum give The four towns St. Joseph Iron Works, Barbee's plat, Fowler's Addition, and Indiana City, platted on the north bank by Joseph Battell and James and Grove Lawrence in June 1836 Industry the iron works built what is said to be the first blast furnace in Indiana and made pig iron from 1834; Wallace Dodge's factory opened in 1878; the Mishawaka Woolen Company, incorporated in 1874, became Ball-Band and then Uniroyal, and closed in 1997 A fire in 1872 a fire burned 49 buildings downtown, and the town then barred wood-frame buildings from the business district County seat no; the county seat of St. Joseph County is South Bend, four miles downriver Worth a visit Battell Park Historic District , Mishawaka Ave., Mishawaka. The city's riverside park, on land once platted as Indiana City and deeded to the town in 1880; the Soldiers' Monument stands there (1884). National Register, 1996. Old Mishawaka Carnegie Library , 122 N. Hill St., Mishawaka. The public library of 1916, built largely with Andrew Carnegie's gift. National Register, 1998. Kamm and Schellinger Brewery , 100 Center St., Mishawaka. The brewery formed in 1880, which brewed until 1951; the old buildings now hold shops and restaurants (100 Center). National Register, 1979. Beiger House (Beiger Mansion) , 317 E. Lincolnway, Mishawaka. The Beiger family mansion on Lincolnway, damaged by fire in 1975 and restored. National Register, 1973. Now an inn and event house. Where the records are Deeds, probate and marriage records are kept by St. Joseph County in South Bend, the county seat. The Mishawaka-Penn-Harris Public Library holds its Local & Family History Collection at the downtown Mishawaka library, with St. Joseph County newspapers on microfilm from 1853, and runs the Mishawaka Memories digital archive. The Mishawaka Enterprise has been published since the 1850s; the South Bend Area Genealogical Society has indexed its legal notices, and the South Bend News-Times (1913–1938) is free on Chronicling America. The History Museum, 808 W. Washington St., South Bend, keeps the county's historical collections. Howard's History of St. Joseph County (1907) gives the town a full chapter. Sources Timothy E. Howard, A History of St. Joseph County, Indiana, vol. 1 (Chicago: Lewis, 1907), ch. t: Who was in town
x: ← The map room Names on the old maps Who was in town Beside each town plan, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed. Here are 331 of those entries from five towns, with the 85 men of Company D, Sixth Michigan Infantry, raised at Dowagiac in 1861, as one roll you can search. Type a surname, a trade or a town. Search the roll 416 entries Elsewhere on the site Turn on JavaScript to search the roll. Each town’s directory can also be read on its plan in the map room . How to read the roll As printed. Names are spelled as the engraver cut them, abbreviations and all: Jas. for James, Wm. for William, Chas. for Charles. A spelling that looks wrong may be the engraver’s, or it may be how the family spelled it then. A question mark after a name means the engraving is worn or crowded and we are not sure of our reading. Look at the plan yourself and tell us what you see. Who is missing. A directory is not a census. It lists people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not here. A handful of entries are also held back because they would give away an answer in the hunt. Every entry links to its map. Open it and find the name in the directory beside the plan. Found someone of your own? A directory line is a start: it puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year. Deeds, censuses, newspapers and probate files can take the story further. We can help. Sources: the business directories printed beside the town plans on the Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien, Michigan (Philadelphia: Geil, Harley & Siverd, 1860), Library of Congress; and on Geil & Harley’s Map of Elkhart Co. Indiana (1861), American Geographical Society Library, University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Libraries. Public domain. Transcribed for Project Scroll. t: Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake
x: ← Front page · All the news Eagle Lake Band night at French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake 2 min read A brass band on folding chairs under the trees, a flag strung overhead, and buggies and motor cars drawn up behind. A summer evening at Eagle Lake, on a card of 1912. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Band concert, French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake, a real-photo postcard of 1912. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Edwardsburg, Mich. The band sits in a ring of folding chairs on the bare ground under the trees. The players wear peaked caps, their music is clipped to stands, and the trombones and the big bass drum stand out among the brass. A flag is strung on a line overhead. Around them the crowd stands close: men in shirtsleeves and straw hats, women in white, and in front one man grinning at the camera with a cigar in his teeth. Behind them are horses and a buggy, and motor cars with their tops up. Documented The words are written across the top of the card: “Band Concert, French’s Hotel, Eagle Lake, Mich.” It is a real-photo postcard of 1912, now in the David V. Tinder Collection at the University of Michigan. No photographer’s name appears on its face. French’s Documented Eagle Lake is in Ontwa Township, Edwardsburg’s own. The village’s history, as the Edwardsburg Chamber tells it, says that in summer “city folks detrained in the village” and were “driven by horse and carriage to French’s Resort on Eagle Lake.” The Edwardsburg Area History Museum has gathered the resort’s life in postcards, many of them provided by Floyd Jerdon of Dowagiac. Its gallery has French’s Landing about 1901 and in 1907, French’s Hotel in 1910 and 1911, another band concert at the resort in 1917, and “Hotel French’s, Eagle Lake Resort” still on a card of 1941. The Eagle Lake Sailing Club says it had its “early beginnings in 1936 at French’s Hotel.” Open questions Open Which band is this: Edwardsburg’s own, a band from Elkhart or South Bend, or the resort’s? Who was the French of French’s, when did the hotel open, and when did it close? Can you name anyone in the crowd? If you know, or if the band played in your family, write to research@projectscroll.com . The museum on Main Street in Edwardsburg is the place to see the rest of the cards. Enjoyed this story? t: Who told Shepard?
x: ← Front page · All the news Case 1 Who told Shepard? Open case 1 min read The only account of the 1846 lodge was written by a man who was a small child when it happened. Somebody told him. Who? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174, where the story is told again. Cassopolis, Mich. Everything we know about the lodge of 1846 comes from one account, written by James M. Shepard and printed in Rogers’s History of Cass County in 1875. Shepard did not see the lodge. He was a small child in 1846 and came to Cassopolis only in September 1868, as the village dentist. When he wrote, about 1875, three of the four charter men could still be found in or near the county: Dr. Evan J. Bonine at Niles, Jordan P. Osborn at Cassopolis, and Dr. Leander Osborn at Vandalia. And he was not sure of everything he had been told. In the 1875 text the founders are “the charter (?) members,” with his own question mark. Mathews, reprinting the passage in 1882, dropped it. So Case 1 asks: who told him? A founder, a member, a guest at the ball, the hotel’s keeper? The answer, if it survives, is in the record: in the books, the papers of the 1870s, or the lives of the men themselves. Case 1 was first opened on 15 October with a different question, whether the lodge ever had a real charter. That question answered itself in Shepard’s own question mark, so the case now asks the one beneath it. Enjoyed this story? t: Fly over Cassopolis, laser point by laser point
x: ← Front page · All the news The map room Fly over Cassopolis, laser point by laser point 1 min read Every laser point of the 2015 survey in the town blocks, the land from Stone Lake to Diamond Lake, story pins, a guided tour, and the sun’s shadows, with the 1860 town plan laid on the ground. Project Scroll · 21 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email Cassopolis in LiDAR: every dot is one laser echo from the 2015 survey. Cassopolis, Mich. In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot in the new model is one of those echoes, from the blocks around the courthouse: 355,650 of them. The buildings and trees stand where the laser found them, 125,189 points of roofs and 230,461 of trees, over the bare ground of the town. Press “1860 plan” and the old town plan from the county wall map is laid on the ground beneath them. Raise the heights, tilt it, fly around it, or go full screen. Documented Updated 23 October. The model now shows every tree and building point the survey kept in the town blocks, about 775,000, and some 760,000 more across the country from Stone Lake to Diamond Lake, on ground shaded from a survey grid one and a half metres apart. Buildings and trees each have their own switch. Gold pins mark the stops of our walking tour; a guided tour flies from Stone Lake to the courthouse square and out to Diamond Lake; tap the ground for its height; and the Sun slider casts every roof’s and tree’s shadow through a midsummer day. Fly over it, and you earn the Laser surveyor badge. Enjoyed this story? Pass it on Know someone who grew up around here, or who loves a good mystery? Send it their way. t: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
x: ← Front page · All the news Soldiers of the valley Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861 From the archive 1 min read Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email Monument Day, Dowagiac, on a real-photo postcard. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Dowagiac, Mich. In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County, under Captain Charles E. Clarke. It became Company D of the Sixth Michigan Infantry. The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge, and joined the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick J. Clarke was killed. It ended the war as heavy artillery, and was discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865. Of its men, four were killed or died of wounds and fifteen died of disease. As in the whole war, sickness killed more of them than battle did. The roll of all 85 men, as Mathews printed it in 1882, is now on the site, checked line by line against the page scans, with this week’s anniversaries from their service. Enjoyed this story? t: Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Dr. Goodwin’s hotel on Broadway Series · 1 of 4 › 2 min read A Civil War cavalry captain who became the village doctor built a hotel on Broadway and kept it himself. It took guests into the 1950s, and nothing of it is left. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Hotel Goodwin, Cassopolis, Mich, 1916, C. R. Childs. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. Three storeys of brick under a mansard roof, with a pointed tower on the corner and HOTEL GOODWIN carved into the parapet. On the card of 1916 a covered wagon and two white horses wait at the kerb, there are striped awnings in the windows, and the last shop on the right has a sign that reads BAKERY. Documented The man behind the name was Dr. Fairfield Israel Goodwin. He served in the Civil War with Taylor’s Chicago Battery, was wounded at Iuka, and then raised Company C of the 8th Michigan Cavalry as its captain. He took his medical degree at the University of Michigan in 1874 and began to practise at Cassopolis the same year. The county history of 1906 says he was also active in real estate, and adds: “He built Hotel Goodwin and is its landlord.” He died in 1918. Reading A walking tour by the county and the Cass District Library’s Local History Branch says he built the hotel probably in 1896–97, in place of an earlier Goodwin hotel of 1887 at 130 South Broadway, a building that still stands. The tour says the Goodwin was a hotel until 1951 and was torn down in the late 1950s or early 1960s. A parking lot in front of Cassopolis Auto Supply is now on the site. Documented In the autumn of 1920 the hotel was badly damaged by fire, most of all inside. The South Bend News-Times called it “Cassopolis’ only hotel.” Two weeks later contractors had nearly finished the roof, and the proprietor, Carrie Ellis, planned to remodel and reopen within a month. Open In 1906 the county history placed the Goodwin House at the north edge of the old public square, on the west side of Broadway. The walking tour places the hotel near the southwest corner of Broadway and State. Which is right? And in what year did the first guest sign the register? Write to research@projectscroll.com . t: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
x: ← Front page · All the news E Clampus Vitus A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846 From the archive Series · 1 of 2 › 37 min read Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis, Michigan, in the spring of 1846: four charter members named, a ball of two hundred badges, and the earliest lodge of the order yet found with its members named. Newspapers of the same year show the order already at work across the state line in Indiana. Here is the whole record, what it does and does not prove, and the questions still open. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 37 min read Share Facebook X Email Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), p. 253. The short version Two county histories, of 1875 and 1882, record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846, with four charter members named and a ball of more than two hundred badges at the Union Hotel. It is the earliest lodge of the order yet found anywhere with its members named. Three of the four founders married sisters of one family. Newspapers of the same year show the order already alive across the state line, in Indiana: at Connersville, at Indianapolis, and at Centreville, whose lodge asked the legislature for a charter and got a joke in the official journal instead. The founders’ family came from Centreville. How the order reached Cassopolis is still an open question. Read the whole story › Cassopolis, Mich. Picture a winter night in the county seat of a frontier county not yet twenty years old. The frame tavern on the square is lit up. Inside, more than two hundred people are wearing the badges of a secret society with a name few of them could have spelled the same way twice: the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus.” It is the winter of 1846–47, and the Cassopolis lodge is less than a year old. In 1875 the first history of Cass County, Michigan, printed a short account of “the first Secret Society, of which there is any record” in the county: a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,” instituted at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846. Seven years later a second county history printed it again. Neither book was written for the order now known as E Clampus Vitus, and so far as we can find, no historian of that order has ever cited either one. A word to the Brethren If you wear the red shirt, you know the story: Ephraim Bee and his commission, Joe Zumwalt carrying the ritual to Hangtown, the lodge at Mokelumne Hill by 1851, and Carl Wheat bringing the order back to life in San Francisco in 1931. You also know the line in the order’s own 1966 history, that by 1849 “the East and Middle West were dotted with Clamper Lodges,” not one of them named. This page names one. It comes with a hall, a ball and four charter members, in the spring of 1846. And the newspapers of that year, just over the state line in Indiana, show the order alive and growing: a lodge at Connersville, a Tent No. 43 at Indianapolis meeting “in full regalia,” and a bill before the legislature to charter a lodge at Centreville. Credo quia absurdum , the motto runs: I believe because it is absurd. Here you will not need to. Every statement below is marked Documented (the record says so), Reading (our interpretation of it) or Open (not yet known), and every source is listed at the foot of the page. At a glance What A lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of Eclampsus Vitus” Where Cassopolis, the county seat of Cass County, Michigan When Instituted in the spring of 1846; collapsed in 1847; revived in 1860 as “The Brothers of Charity” Charter members Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. t: E Clampus Vitus: the complete record
x: ← Front page · All the news E Clampus Vitus E Clampus Vitus: the complete record Discovery · 6 new findings › Series · 2 of 2 › 49 min read Every lodge of the order on record before 1905, from Indiana in 1846 to Sierraville in 1904, each with its earliest source; the words and customs of the old order; the revival of 1931 and the chapters today; the myths set beside the record; and the founding documents in full. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 49 min read Share Facebook X Email Mokelumne Hill, home of Lodge No. 1001, from Stockton Hill, 1866. Lawrence & Houseworth stereograph; Library of Congress (public domain). The short version In 1966 the historians of E Clampus Vitus wished that someone would one day compile a complete list of the order’s early lodges. This page is that list: 61 places where the order is on record before 1905, from Connersville, Indiana, in February 1846 and Cassopolis, Michigan, that spring, to California from 1852 and on to Hawaii, each with its earliest surviving source. Inbody’s camera 2 min read A meat market and a bakery, a druggist selling ice cream soda next to the post office, and a frame school with a bell tower. Three cards by an Indiana photographer who made picture postcards. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Elkhart St., Edwardsburg, Mich., a real-photo postcard of 1910, “Copr., Inbody.” Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Edwardsburg, Mich. About 1910 a photographer came to Edwardsburg and made three views of the village. Each card has its caption printed in white along the bottom, and each ends with the same two words: “Copr., Inbody.” All three are now at the Library of Congress. Documented Elkhart St. A row of frame stores with tin awnings. On the left, the window of a shop selling tobacco and cigars; next along, a sign for a MEAT MARKET and another for a BAKERY. A bicycle leans at the edge of the walk, a man stands under an awning, and a horse and wagon wait further down the street. Documented Post office. The village post office sits in a low frame building beside a brick corner store whose sign reads “B. C. Fisk, Druggist.” Its awnings advertise ICE CREAM SODA and CIGARS. Three people stand at the post office door, and on the fence to the left are show bills dated the 18th of June. The post office itself was old by then: the Chamber’s history says it was set up on 4 December 1828 as St. Joseph, renamed Edwardsburgh on 1 February 1830, closed for a time, restored on 23 August 1841, and lost its final “h” on a postmaster’s order in 1845. Reading Public school. A two-storey frame school with a pedimented front and a bell tower on the roof, standing in an open yard among young trees. The Chamber’s history says a two-storey frame school was built on the north side of Church Street in 1861, and a new brick school on Section Street in 1923. The card is probably the school of 1861, but we have not proved it. Our gallery has a second view of the same building, an Inbody card of 1911. Who was J. Inbody? Documented John Inbody, born 16 June 1866 and died 10 June 1915. On the back of his own portrait, taken about 1890 at A. J. Dawdy’s studio in Goshen, someone wrote: “He was a photographer, made picture postcards.” The Library of Congress catalogues one of his cards as published by “J. Inbody, Elkhart, Ind.” The site’s gallery holds his cards of Cassopolis, Edwardsburg, Elkhart, Goshen, Bristol and Pine Lake at La Porte, from 1909 to 1915. He worked the valley on both sides of the state line. Open Who kept the meat market and the bakery? What show was coming on 18 June? Zoom in on the cards: the smaller signs are there to be read. The other half is stranger. The county seat was first somewhere else, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain, and the village was spelled with an A for nearly forty years. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 10 min read Share Facebook X Email The plan of “Cassapolis” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division. Cassopolis, Mich. Ask how Cassopolis got its name and the answer comes quickly: it is the city of Cass, named for Lewis Cass, governor of Michigan Territory, with the Greek word for a city on the end. That much is true. But the county seat was first at another village, the man who won it for Stone Lake is said to have walked through a night of cold rain to do it, and for nearly forty years the post office spelled the name with an A. We went back to the county’s three histories, of 1875, 1882 and 1906, to Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838, and to the hand-coloured county map of 1860, to see what the record shows and what is only a good story. The act says only “the name thereof shall be Cass.” That it honours Lewis Cass is understood, not written. The county seat came first to Geneva, on Diamond Lake, in 1830. A new commission moved it in 1831. The village was platted in 1831 as “Cassapolis,” with an A, and proclaimed the county seat on 19 December 1831. Three streets on the plat carry the commissioners’ names: Disbrow, Rowland and O’Keefe. The O came slowly. “Cassopolis” is in print by 1838, but the post office kept “Cassapolis” until 1870, and the county map of 1860 still letters the village “Cassapolis.” What it does not show, yet The plat and the governor’s proclamation themselves. We have read them only as the county histories report them. Who chose the name, and why “-polis.” Why the A became an O. The 1906 history thought it was for the sound. Story or record? It was made almost at once, in 1848, when the Michigan Central Railroad came through and two men laid out a village beside the depot. x: ← Front page · All the news How the towns got their names How Kalamazoo got its name Myth tested Series · 7 of 7 › Go see it 28 min read Everyone in Kalamazoo knows two stories: a footrace against a boiling pot, and a founder run out of town over a stolen cherry tree. We went back to the record, from a Jesuit’s route notes of about 1760 to the act of 1836, to see where each story really starts, where the letter L came from, and what the Potawatomi names for the place and the river say today. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 28 min read Share Facebook X Email William Greason, Bayou on the Kalamazoo River, Douglas, oil on canvas, 1934. Public domain (Wikimedia Commons). The short version Everyone in Kalamazoo knows two stories: a runner racing a boiling pot, and a founder run out of town over a stolen cherry tree. The name itself came from the river, and it is old: a Jesuit wrote “kikanamaso” in his route notes about 1760. The L came later, first in the treaty of 1821; the Potawatomi language has no L sound. The village of Bronson became Kalamazoo by an act of the legislature in 1836. The race story was in print by 1867, but the runner’s name, his bride and the year 1810 first appear in a newspaper of 1922. The cherry tree has no early source at all. We trace each story to where it starts, and give the Potawatomi names for the place and the river in use today. Read the whole story › Kalamazoo, Mich. Ask anyone in Kalamazoo why the city is called Kalamazoo and you will hear about a footrace: a young man running to the river and back before a pot of water boiled away. Ask why it is not still called Bronson and you will hear about a stolen cherry tree. You will find both on the city’s own website. Neither one, it turns out, rests where people think it does. We went back to the paper: a Jesuit’s route notes of about 1760, a French map of 1744, the treaty of 1821, an atlas map of 1822, the act of the legislature that changed the name in 1836, the county’s first histories, and the linguists who have argued over the word for 170 years. Then we set beside them the names that the Potawatomi people use for the place and the river today. The record does not hand over a single tidy answer. It does show which stories are old, which are new, where the letter L came from, and which explanation has the oldest written support. But “pawpaw” is not a Native word, the village was laid out as Paw Paw, not Lafayette, and the first Paw Paw in local government was in the next county. We went back to the record. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 7 min read Share Facebook X Email The plan of Paw Paw, “County Seat of Van Buren Co.,” on Geil, Harley & Siverd’s Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien (Philadelphia, 1860), detail. Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division. Paw Paw, Mich. Paw Paw takes its name from the Paw Paw River, and the river from the pawpaw, the small native tree with the big tropical-tasting fruit that grew, the county history says, thickly along its banks. So far, so simple. But the county history says the river was “named by the Indians,” and pawpaw is an English word; many people believe the village was first called Lafayette, though it was laid out as Paw Paw; and the first place in local government to be called Paw Paw was in Berrien County. We went back to the county history of 1880, the federal place-names list of 1905, the state’s historical marker at the courthouse and the county map of 1860 to see what the record shows. The township took the village’s name on 15 March 1867. The post office opened in 1835 under Peter Gremps; the county seat came in 1837. The first civil “Paw Paw” was in Berrien County, a township erected in 1831 on the same river. What it does not show, yet Any Native-language name of the river, in a published source. t: How Vandalia got its name
x: ← Front page · All the news How the towns got their names How Vandalia got its name Series · 6 of 7 › Go see it 8 min read No source we have read explains why Vandalia is called Vandalia. The record shows a post office in 1850, a grist mill, a plat in 1851, and a creek named in 1822 by a missionary for his wife. Here is what is known, and the guesses that are not. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 8 min read Share Facebook X Email The Old Mill, Vandalia, Mich., real-photo postcard, about 1908–1918. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Vandalia, Mich. Some town names explain themselves, and some are explained in every county history. Vandalia is neither. It grew up around a grist mill on a creek in Penn Township, it had a post office called Vandalia by 1850, and its plat was filed early in 1851. Who chose the name, and why, no source we have read explains. So this is a story about what the record does show, and about the guesses that fill the gap. We went back to the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, Michigan’s first gazetteer of 1838 and the post-office lists. At a glance The place Vandalia, Michigan: a village in Penn Township, Cass County, on Christiann Creek Post office 1850, the first record of the name The mill A grist mill of 1849 on the creek, “the nucleus for the village of Vandalia” The plat Laid out by Stephen Bogue and Charles P. Ball, 3 January 1851 (Rogers, 1875); filed 21 February 1851 (Glover, 1906) Incorporated 1875 The creek Named in 1822 by the missionary Isaac McCoy for his wife, Christiana Why it matters The village name has no recorded reason; the creek beside it does The case in brief What the record shows The name is first on record for a post office, in 1850. The village grew around a grist mill built on the creek in 1849 by two Quaker settlers, Stephen Bogue and Charles P. Ball, who laid out the village in 1851. The plat followed in 1851: laid out on 3 January, Rogers says; filed on 21 February, Glover says. The creek had its name first, from the missionary Isaac McCoy, who named it in 1822 for his wife. What it does not show, yet Who chose “Vandalia,” and why. Neither the 1875 nor the 1906 county history says. Whether the name came from Vandalia, Illinois, as many assume. Story or record? Play along Here are eight things people say about the name. For each, make your call: true, false, or no record either way. Then see what the paper shows. “Vandalia, Michigan, was named after Vandalia, Illinois.” No record It is the usual guess, and it may be right: the Illinois town had been the state capital and was well known by 1850. But neither the 1875 nor the 1906 county history explains the name. “Vandalia comes from a Native-language word.” No record No source gives it a Native origin. It is a Latin-style European name, “land of the Vandals,” used for towns across the country. “There was a Vandalia post office before there was a village plat.” True Postal listings date the Vandalia office from 1850; the village was laid out in January 1851. “The village grew up around a grist mill.” True Glover, in 1906: the grist mill on Christiann Creek “served as the nucleus for the village of Vandalia.” “The creek through Vandalia was named for a missionary’s wife.” True Rogers, 1875: “It was so named by the missionary in honor of his wife, as they crossed it the 18th of December.” The 1882 history names him: the Rev. x: ← Front page · All the news Mishawaka City Hall, Mishawaka, and the mayor on the card 1 min read A postcard of 1910 names the building and the man in charge of it. Who was Mayor Herzog, and where did his city hall go? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email City Hall, Mishawaka, Ind., Mayor Herzog. Postcard, 1910. Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division. Mishawaka, Ind. The card was made in 1910, and its captions do two jobs at once: “City Hall, Mishawaka, Ind.” and, under a portrait set into the sky, “Mayor Herzog.” The building was only six years old. The city had put it up in 1904 at First and Church Streets. Mishawaka was a young city, too. Its voters had turned the town into a city in 1899 and chosen Manuel Fisher as the first mayor. By the census of 1910 the city held 11,886 people, more than twice as many as in 1900. A new high school and St. Joseph Hospital both opened that year. The mayor Documented He was John A. Herzog, a Democrat, elected in November 1909; the papers printed his name in their lists of the new mayors across Indiana. Herzog was also State Chief Ranger of the Catholic Order of Foresters, and in July 1911 an Indiana paper introduced him as “State Chief Ranger John A. Herzog, mayor of Mishawaka.” The Foresters chose him again in June 1913. That autumn an earlier mayor, Melville W. Mix, ran again, and the South Bend News-Times said Mix would take up the work “continued along the same lines by Mayor Herzog.” In the election of November 1913 Mix lost by 423 votes to Ralph W. Gaylor, who ran as an independent. Where did it go? Open The South Bend Tribune wrote in 2022 that an older city hall on Church Street had stood where the police station is now, and that the city moved its offices to the old Bingham school in 1984. Today City Hall is at 100 Lincolnway West. Was the Church Street building the one on this card? When did it come down? If you know, write to research@projectscroll.com . Enjoyed this story? t: Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Race day at the Cassopolis fair grounds Series · 4 of 4 › 2 min read A horse and sulky on the track, a crowd at the rail and a covered grandstand behind. Whose track was it, and where did the county fair run its races? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Race Track at Cassopolis, Mich., about 1905–1918. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph taken on the track itself. Men in hats and dark suits stand along the left. A horse in harness, hitched to a light sulky, is being led along the dirt. To the right is a raised judges’ stand, and beyond it a long line of people at the rail. Under the trees at the far end the dust hangs in the air. Documented The Cass County Agricultural Society was organised in the spring of 1851 and held its first fair that fall. According to the 1906 county history, its grounds had to move three times because of “the right of eminent domain.” Until 1857 the fairs were held on Samuel Graham’s land at Cassopolis. The railroads then took two sites in turn, and in 1871 the society bought twenty acres from Samuel Graham in the north part of the village for $3,000. After the 1884 fair a mortgage on the grounds was foreclosed, and the village of Cassopolis bought the land. In 1906 the village still owned it. Documented The society held no fairs after 1884. Then, in 1905, “a new organization was effected and held a successful fair.” The Billboard listed the Cassopolis fair for 22 to 25 September 1908. A harness-racing paper of 1916 records a horse that had started at Cassopolis in 1911. Documented The fair then stopped for three years. In October 1915 the South Bend News-Times reported that the Grangers had brought it back. Tents went up on the Cassopolis fair grounds again, the association got “the neglected race track” into shape, and the state master of the Grange spoke from the grandstand. Baseball and a motorcycle race came first, with horse races to follow on the Thursday and Friday. Open Was the track on this card the village’s twenty acres of 1871? Is any of it under today’s fairgrounds on North O’Keefe Street, where the Cass County Fair is still held? If you can place the grandstand, or you have a race programme from these years, write to research@projectscroll.com . Enjoyed this story? t: Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities
x: ← Front page · All the news Between two cities Springbrook Park, halfway between two cities 2 min read For more than sixty years the park on the river between South Bend and Mishawaka gave the valley baseball, a summer theatre, band concerts and rides. Very little of it is left. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Springbrook Park, South Bend, Ind. Postcard by The Indiana News Company, about 1910. St. Joseph County Public Library (South Bend, IN). South Bend, Ind. In 1901 a Walkerton paper put it in one line: Springbrook Park lay “midway between South Bend and Mishawaka.” It stood on the St. Joseph River, on what is now Lincolnway East. On the card a crowd in summer white walks along a pond, with a pavilion and the frame of a ride behind them. Documented Baseball came early. In June 1896 a team was to play all its games “on the new diamond at Springbrook Park,” and in 1897 the South Bend “Senators” played Whiting there. The railway’s park In June 1899 the papers reported that a vaudeville theatre would be built at the park, and in March 1901 that the railway company would put up a new summer theatre. By 1904 there were matinees at the Springbrook Park Casino. In April 1907, under the headline “White City for South Bend,” the Walkerton Independent reported that the Chicago, South Bend & Northern Indiana Railway, “which owns Springbrook park,” had leased it for ten years to the Interurban Amusement Company, which promised a big theatre, a dancing pavilion and other attractions. In the summer of 1914 there were Sunday band concerts, and families came out for picnic suppers. Playland Reading In the 1920s Earl J. “Pete” Redden took over the park and held a contest to rename it, and the winning name was Playland Park. The ballpark stayed. In the years after the Second World War the South Bend Blue Sox of the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League played their home games there. Open The park closed about 1960, and the land later became a golf course and then student housing for Indiana University South Bend. Pieces of the concrete grandstand are said to remain. Did you ride at Playland, or see the Blue Sox play? Do you know the year the gates closed for good? Write to research@projectscroll.com . Enjoyed this story? The village of Cassopolis was laid out on its shore in 1831, the county history of 1882 called it the most peculiar lake in the county, and people once believed it rose and fell with Lake Superior. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 9 min read Share Facebook X Email Stone Lake and the village on the Plan of Cassopolis in the Atlas of Cass County, Michigan (Philadelphia, 1872), detail. Internet Archive. Cassopolis, Mich. Stone Lake lies at the foot of Broadway in Cassopolis, close enough to the courthouse that the village was laid out around its shore. It is not large, and it is not famous. But it has puzzled people for a long time. No stream runs into it, and none runs out. Its water was soft when its neighbor’s was hard. And in the 1880s, by the county history’s account, many people in Cass County believed it was fed by an underground river from Lake Superior. We went back to the county histories of 1882 and 1906 and the county atlas of 1872 to see what the record says about the lake, and what it still keeps to itself. It has no visible inlet or outlet, and its water was “very fine and very soft” in 1882, when Diamond Lake’s was hard. People believed in a river from Lake Superior. The 1882 history reports the belief that the lake was fed by “the great subterranean stream” from Superior, and rose and fell with it. The village was laid out on its shore, and for years drew its drinking water from it. What it does not show, yet Whether the lake still rises and falls when its neighbors don’t. t: Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island
x: ← Front page · All the news Diamond Lake Summer on Diamond Lake: Forest Hall and the island 3 min read A tennis net on the lawn, a windmill over the roof and the name along the ridge: Forest Hall, 1909. Across the water, a hotel on an island, with a cannon on its grass. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 3 min read Share Facebook X Email Forest Hall, Diamond Lake, Cassopolis, a real-photo postcard of 1909 published by O. L. Yerty, Cassopolis. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. A tennis net is stretched across the lawn. Players stand at the net with their rackets, others watch from the shade, and a windmill stands above the roof. Along the ridge, in big letters, is the name: FOREST HALL. The card was published in 1909 by O. L. Yerty of Cassopolis, and the caption on its face reads “Forest Hall – Diamond Lake.” What Forest Hall was Reading The Diamond Lake Association keeps a timeline of the lake, compiled by Jean Schultz from local sources and crediting Lois Webster Welch’s book A Diamond Sparkles . It says the house began in 1872 as “The Chicago House,” a vacation home on the north shore built by three officials of the Michigan Central Railroad. In 1880 it was renamed Forest Hall and leased as a public resort, and in 1891 a Mr. Rudd and a Dr. Laughton bought it and made it a health resort. A nine-hole golf course was laid out on its grounds in 1921. Forest Hall closed as a resort hotel in 1926 but stayed on as the clubhouse of the Diamond Lake Golf Club, and in 1935 it was torn down and its wood used to build a new clubhouse. Documented The county history of 1906 bears out the date of 1891. In the life of the hotel’s proprietor, Glover writes: “In 1891 he purchased the Forest Hall Hotel, which he has since been conducting.” He adds that the hotel had become “a favorite summer resort.” Forest Hall was not alone. The association’s timeline counts five resort hotels on the lake by 1900, and Glover describes another of them, Shore Acres, as “an attractive summer hotel.” The island Documented The island was known long before the hotels. Mathews, in 1882, gives Diamond Lake an area of 1,083 acres, and he gives a section of his book to Job Wright, “the recluse of Diamond Lake Island,” and tells of Wright’s prediction of “Harrison’s early death.” The association’s timeline says Wright built a log cabin on the island in 1829 and lived there until he died in 1842. Reading Then the summer crowds came. By the association’s timeline, picnic parties were going over to the island in 1873. In 1878 Fred Moon and Colonel Allen built a croquet court, a roller skating rink, an outdoor dance platform and an amphitheater there, and the Cassopolis Vigilant reported in 1879 that there were now enough buildings on the island “to shelter 5000 people from storms.” In 1889 Captain John Bartlett bought the island and took over the Diamond Lake Island Hotel. The hotel closed in 1919, and in 1925 the island was platted for sale as residential lots. Open One postcard in the strip at the top of this site is captioned “The Island House, Diamond Lake, Cassopolis”: a long frame building with a deep porch, young trees along the path, and a field gun on its wheels on the lawn. Was the Island House the same building as the Diamond Lake Island Hotel? Was that the gun fired on the Fourth of July in 1882, when the timeline says the island celebrated “by shooting off fireworks and artillery”? And who was the proprietor Glover wrote about? His life begins on page 755 of Glover. If you know, or have a card or a photograph, write to research@projectscroll.com . Enjoyed this story? What the record says about the James E. Bonine House, and what it has yet to show. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 24 min read Share Facebook X Email James E. Bonine’s farm as the county history described it in 1882: History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago, 1882), p. 251. Internet Archive. The short version The brick house with the mansard tower on M-60 west of Vandalia was the home of James E. Bonine, a Quaker farmer from Indiana with 1,600 acres, who married into the Bogue family whose farm the Kentucky raiders struck in 1847. His elk park was famous: the county history says elk went to the King of Italy, and an Italian report of 1871 tells of the king’s agent buying elk in America. The herd outlived him by more than fifty years. The record shows a family of anti-slavery Quakers. It does not yet show, in any document of the 1840s or 1850s, James E. Bonine or his house at work on the Underground Railroad; that story rests on the society that keeps the house and on local tradition. Here is what is documented, what is told, and what is still to find. Read the whole story › Vandalia, Mich. At the corner of M-60 and Penn Road, just west of Vandalia, stands a brick house with a tall mansard tower, and across the highway a small Gothic carriage house. They were built, by the society’s account, by James E. Bonine, a Quaker farmer whose family came to Young’s Prairie from Indiana in the 1840s, and since 2010 they have belonged to the Underground Railroad Society of Cass County, which opens them to visitors and tells the story of the freedom seekers who passed through this country before the Civil War. The house is now the best-known Underground Railroad site in the county. We went back to the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906, and to the first national list of Underground Railroad workers, to see what the record says about the Bonines, the house and the farm around it. t: The courthouse that became the Colonial
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis The courthouse that became the Colonial Then & now Series · 2 of 4 › 1 min read The Colonial Opera House on a card of 1913 had served Cass County as its courthouse for more than half a century before it was moved across the village. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email The Colonial Opera House, Cassopolis, Mich., 1913. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. A white frame building with tall columns, a pediment and a domed cupola. Across the front, in capitals: THE COLONIAL. The caption, written across the foot of the card, reads “Colonial Opera House, Cassopolis, Mich.” The card dates from 1913. Documented The building was older than it looks. It was the county’s second courthouse, a two-storey frame building finished in 1841, and for more than half a century it stood on the northeast quarter of the public square. When the stone courthouse replaced it, it was sold and moved to the south side of State Street, west of Broadway. In 1906 the county history found it there “used as a storage house.” Documented By the time of the card it was a place of entertainment. In April 1917 the high school chorus gave a comic operetta at “the Colonial theater.” The Film Daily Year Book of 1927 lists the Colonial at Cassopolis with 476 seats. It was remodelled in 1937 as the Gem Theatre, showed films until 1960, and was torn down in 1968. Open When did the old courthouse become an opera house? A theatre history says it opened as the Colonial Opera House in 1899, with 420 seats, and became the Colonial Theatre in 1909. But the county history of 1906 calls it a storage house. And where did the name come from? In 1906 the historian wrote that its lines combined “the Greek temple with Colonial residences.” If you have a programme, a ticket or a diary entry that settles it, write to research@projectscroll.com . t: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
x: ← Front page · All the news From 1923 The day 3,000 people came to watch one log 1 min read Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email The card of 1923, Building the Pioneer Log Cabin. Private collection. Cassopolis, Mich. At half past eight on the morning of 23 May 1923, a black walnut log twenty-six feet long was carried to its place by twenty-four men. A band played and the crowd sang. About three thousand people stood and watched, and many had driven up to fifty miles to be there. It was the first log of the Cass County Pioneer Log Cabin. A note written on the back of one card of the day says fifty-two volunteers did the first morning’s work. The logs came from families across the county, given from their own land. Each log was numbered, and a list kept the family’s name, the town and the kind of tree. The card printed for the occasion gives the whole job in one line: May 23 to June 20, 1923. Four weeks, from the first log to Pioneer Day. The cabin still stands in Cassopolis today, as the Pioneer Log Cabin Museum. Enjoyed this story? The old hotel stood at the northwest corner of Broadway and State Street, at the heart of the village. It was the Union Hotel, where the lodge of 1846 held its grand ball. x: ← Front page · All the news Lore and legend The Indian Lake Sea Serpent: Twelve Feet Long, and Shy Go see it 8 min read In October 1898 a “huge sea serpent” terrorized the cottagers on Indian Lake, near Dowagiac, and men went out with guns to hunt it. Two weeks later the papers said it was an otter and a fish. The next summer it was back, twelve feet long. We read every report we could find, on the page. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 23 October 2026 · 8 min read Share Facebook X Email The short version In October 1898 Michigan papers reported that cottagers on Indian Lake, five miles west of Dowagiac, had been “terrorized of late by a huge sea serpent,” and that parties were out with guns to hunt it. Two weeks later the same columns said it “proved to be an otter and a muskalonge.” In July 1899 it was reported again: about twelve feet long, fast “like an arrow,” and so shy that hardly anyone had seen it close. Every report came through the state-news columns, so all of them together are really one witness. The lake has a stream in and a stream out, and the state had stocked it with 400,000 walleye fry the year before. Who first reported it, and who decided it was an otter, is still open. Read the whole story › Indian Lake, Mich. In the autumn of 1898, something in a lake five miles west of Dowagiac frightened the cottagers so badly that men went out with guns to hunt it. The papers called it a sea serpent. Two weeks later they said it was nothing of the kind. And then, the next summer, it came back. The story ran in newspapers all over Michigan, a line or two at a time. We went back and read every one of them we could find, on the page. Nobody we can find ever saw the serpent up close. October 1898: something in the lake Documented The first word we can find is a single line in the Grand Traverse Herald of 13 October 1898, in its round-up of news from around the state: “Indian lake cottagers, near Dowagiac, were terrorized by an enormous sea serpent. Public domain Documented The next day the same news reached Mount Pleasant. The Isabella County Enterprise of 14 October put it this way: “Residents of the vicinity of Indian lake, near Dowagiac, have been terrorized of late by a huge sea serpent in the lake.” The Clare Sentinel ran the same words that day, and the Saline Observer a few days later. “Terrorized of late”: the Isabella County Enterprise , Mount Pleasant, 14 October 1898, p. 4. Digital Michigan Newspapers, Clarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University. Public domain Reading “Of late” is the telling phrase. Whatever it was, it had been seen more than once before anyone sent the story out of the county. t: The Kentucky Raid of 1847
x: ← Front page · All the news The Underground Railroad The Kentucky Raid of 1847 Myth tested Series · 2 of 2 › Go see it 19 min read In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians came to the Quaker farms of Cass County to carry nine people back into slavery. Their neighbors stopped them at O’Dell’s mill, a hearing at Cassopolis set the nine free, and the lawsuits ran on for five years. We went back to the papers of 1847, the court files and the county histories. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 19 min read Share Facebook X Email The chapter heading in Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis, 1875), p. 131. Internet Archive. The short version In August 1847, a dozen or more men from northern Kentucky came to the Quaker farms of Cass County and seized nine people who had escaped from slavery. Several hundred neighbors stopped them near O’Dell’s mill, where Vandalia is now, and took everyone to Cassopolis. There a commissioner set the nine free, because no certified copy of Kentucky’s slave laws was offered in evidence. Fifty-two freedom seekers then left for Canada. The slaveholders sued the Quakers in federal court at Detroit; the jury disagreed in 1851, two men settled, and the last suits were dismissed in 1852. We went back to the papers of 1847 and the court files, and found details the later histories missed, including what the raiders’ own home paper said about their bail. Read the whole story › Cassopolis, Mich. In the summer of 1847 a party of Kentuckians rode into Cass County to take back people who had escaped from slavery and were living and working on the Quaker farms around Young’s Prairie. In one night they seized nine. By the next morning the neighbors had caught up with them near O’Dell’s mill, at what is now Vandalia, and a crowd of several hundred walked raiders and captives together to Cassopolis. There a county commissioner heard the case and set the nine free, and that same day a party of fifty-two started north for Canada. The story is told every year in Cass County, and some of what is told has grown in the telling. We went back to what was written at the time: the Covington, Kentucky, newspaper that spoke for the raiders, the federal court papers, a freedom seeker’s own account, and the county histories of 1875, 1882 and 1906. t: The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur
x: ← Front page · All the news Near Decatur The Newton House, a farmhouse museum near Decatur 2 min read One family lived in this Volinia Township house from 1844 to 1930. Today it is a museum, open on the first Sunday of each month from June to September. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien, Michigan, published by Geil, Harley & Siverd, Philadelphia, 1860. Library of Congress. Volinia Township, Mich. On the 1860 wall map of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien counties, Volinia is the third township along the top row of Cass County. Directly above it, across the heavy county line, is Decatur Township in Van Buren County, and the plan of Decatur village is one of the small insets on the map’s left side. In Volinia, on the Marcellus Highway, stands the Newton House. The house Documented By the Cass County Historical Society’s account, the house was “built by Colonel James Newton in 1844.” In 1868 his son George Newton “commissioned the architect Christian Haefner to design and build an addition,” and the house is “a fine example of nineteenth century Italianate architecture.” The family lived in it until 1930. The state marker on the road, put up in 1977, puts it more briefly: “Designed by Christian Haefner in the 1860s, this house belonged to George Newton, a state legislator.” Documented Rogers’s county history of 1875 has the Newtons’ lives. Colonel James Newton was born in England in 1777, came to America as a boy and moved to Ohio in 1804. George was born in Preble County, Ohio, in 1810 and came to Michigan with his father in 1831. George taught the first school in the Higgins schoolhouse, the winter after it was built in 1836, and in 1858 he was elected to the state legislature. Documented In 1931 Fred Russ bought the house and the timberland around it, and in 1942 the land went to Michigan State University as a gift. It became the Fred Russ Experimental Forest, 580 acres, and the house was restored by the Cass County Historical Commission. A 40-acre stand of oak and hickory in the forest, named Newton Woods after George Newton, was made a National Natural Landmark in 1976. The house was entered on the state register of historic sites in 1974 and on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. Visiting The Newton House is at 20689 Marcellus Highway, Decatur, and opens its doors on the first Sunday of each month from June to September, 1:00 to 4:30 pm. The 2026 season is over; check the society’s website before you go next summer. Its rooms show daily life across the years the Newtons lived there, and several are set aside for reading and research on the family, the woods around the house and local history. The county has leased the house from the university since 1980; in June 2026 the university’s trustees agreed to sell it to the historical society, and we have not yet been able to confirm that the sale has closed. One more thing to try: open the 1860 map, find Volinia, and see whether the Newton name is on its farms. Enjoyed this story? t: The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel
x: ← Front page · All the news South Bend The night 3,000 were invited to the Oliver Hotel 2 min read James Oliver, the plow maker, built South Bend a grand hotel at Main and Washington. It opened the week before Christmas 1899 and stood until 1967. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Oliver Hotel, South Bend, Indiana. Postcard by the E. C. Kropp Co., Milwaukee, before 1917. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. South Bend, Ind. On the evening of 20 December 1899 the new Oliver Hotel held its first reception. About three thousand invitations had gone out, to South Bend, Chicago and other cities. Palms and cut flowers filled the rooms, a buffet supper was served all evening, and every part of the house was open for guests to look over. The next day it opened to the public. The host was James Oliver, the South Bend plow maker. With him stood his wife, his son Joseph D. Oliver and his wife, and his only daughter and her husband, George Ford. The Indianapolis Journal ’s man in South Bend called it “probably the largest” reception ever given in the city. Built for the plow trade Customers of the plow works came to South Bend from overseas, and until then, the History Museum says, there was nowhere fit to put them up. So the Olivers built a hotel themselves. The first stone of the foundation was laid in July 1898 at the northwest corner of Main and Washington Streets, and James Oliver, then in his seventies, watched over most of the work. The hotel had 250 guest rooms, and its first manager was Charles Baur, who had come from Terre Haute. It made its own electricity, with three dynamos to light 1,700 lamps. The lobby and rotunda were done in the Italian Renaissance style and trimmed with gold, and sixteen painted women at the top of the rotunda stood for the seasons, the arts and the four elements. The South Bend Tribune called it “the most magnificent hotel in Indiana.” What became of it In later years it was the Pick-Oliver. Its big sign was taken down in November 1957, and in the late summer of 1967 the wrecking ball brought the building down while people on the sidewalk watched. A bank tower went up on the corner, and it is now the Chase Tower. Open Did you stay at the Oliver, or eat in its dining room? Do you have a menu, a key or a piece of its china? t: Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac
x: ← Front page · All the news Dowagiac, 1912 Five minutes with Roosevelt at Dowagiac 2 min read On Saturday, 30 March 1912, Theodore Roosevelt’s train stopped at Dowagiac on its way across Michigan. Oscar C. Haight’s camera caught the crowd. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Roosevelt Special, March 30th 1912. Real-photo postcard by Oscar C. Haight. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Dowagiac, Mich. The news came the day before. As the Dowagiac museum’s Steve Arseneau retold it in 2016 from the Dowagiac Daily News , the paper called it an “exclusive announcement”: the former president would halt his special train in Dowagiac “and make a five minute speech from the rear platform.” Few people in the town had ever seen him. It was Saturday, 30 March 1912, and Roosevelt was campaigning to take the Republican nomination from President Taft. The stores were to close for the visit. A whistle at the water works was to sound when the train left Niles, and the interurban from Benton Harbor and St. Joseph ran a special schedule to bring people in from Berrien County. Late, and brief The train had left Chicago late and came in about an hour behind time, at half past three. Roosevelt began, as the paper reported it, “Ladies, gentlemen and babies,” and spoke for about five minutes, mostly about a bill to give Michigan a primary election. He wished he could stay longer, the paper said, but all he could say was “good luck and good bye.” The Daily News headline read “Monster Crowd Sees Roosevelt: Colonel Talks For 5 Minutes.” Twelve hours in Michigan Documented Dowagiac was one stop on a long day. A wire story printed in Michigan papers the next week said the colonel put in “12 strenuous hours” in the state, with speeches from the car platform at Kalamazoo, Battle Creek and Ann Arbor. That night he spoke for an hour at the Light Guard armory in Detroit. The hall was full an hour early, about a thousand people waited in the street, and it was announced from the stage that he would speak to them from a balcony of the Hotel Cadillac. Haight’s card, signed “Haight Photo.”, shows the crowd packed across the tracks by the depot, with the train at the right. Open Is your family in that crowd? t: The True Story of the Dewey Lake Monster: The Week the Valley Went Wild
x: ← Front page · All the news Lore and legend The True Story of the Dewey Lake Monster: The Week the Valley Went Wild Discovery · 5 new findings › Go see it 57 min read Everyone around Sister Lakes knows the story of the 1964 monster. Most of what they know is wrong. It did not begin with berry pickers, and it did not begin in 1964: a hundred and twenty-five years earlier, someone peeled the bark from a tree at a fork in the road to Dewey’s Lake and wrote a warning on it in red chalk. This is the real story, and it is stranger than the legend. By Michael Urbanski · Project Scroll · 23 October 2026 · 57 min read Share Facebook X Email The 1964 scare was real. The short version The legend says some berry pickers saw a ten-foot monster in 1964 and the sheriff found nothing. The record says more. People near Dewey Lake, west of Dowagiac, had been seeing a large, hairy thing on two legs since 1962. On 9 June 1964 it was seen between a barn and a shed on a farm south of the lake: about nine feet, five hundred pounds, red eyes, a cry like a baby. Two days later three girls saw it cross a road in broad daylight, and one fainted. For a week the Sister Lakes country went wild: armed hunters from three states, a $1,000 reward, “Monster Burgers,” and migrant families sleeping locked in their cars. The papers called it nonexistent. But the story is far older than 1964. The county’s oldest books hold older frights: a blood-drinking “monster” cat, a serpent in neighboring Indian Lake, and a warning chalked in red on a tree at a fork in the road. Read against the old township map, that warning, “Turn to the left and go to the Devil,” pointed down the road to Dewey’s Lake. And the reports from this valley have never quite stopped. Read the whole story › Sister Lakes, Mich. You have probably heard the story. In 1964 some berry pickers near Dowagiac saw a hairy monster, ten feet tall. The papers had a laugh, the sheriff found nothing, and that was the end of it. Almost none of that is true. It was not one sighting. People had been seeing the thing, and keeping quiet about it, for two years before anyone called the police. It was not ten feet tall, not at first: the first accounts on the wire said nine, and a girl who saw it in broad daylight said seven, and it grew with every newspaper that printed it. It did not begin with pickers in a strawberry field. It began after dark at a farmhouse south of Dewey Lake, between a barn and a shed, where a woman said the thing had been coming around for summers, and had once chased her into her own house. And nobody in 1964 called it Bigfoot. That word was only six years old, coined by a California newspaper in 1958. In Sister Lakes they called it the monster, or the creature, or the thing. The papers decided within a week that there was nothing there. But the story did not begin in 1964, and the strangest parts of it were never in the papers. They are in the county’s own oldest books. A hundred and twenty-five years before the berry pickers, someone peeled the bark from a tree on the road to “Dewey’s Lake” and wrote a warning on it in red chalk. An 1882 history called a thing in these woods “the monster” and said it drank a colt’s blood. In 1898 the lake next door had a serpent of its own. And the reports kept coming, from the swamps and creeks and woods of this valley, long after everyone agreed there was nothing out there. This is the real story, as the record tells it. The St. Joseph River valley. For a century the towns of the valley made things the whole country knew by name. Round Oak stoves came out of Dowagiac from 1871. x: ← Front page · All the news Where is this? A depot, a water tower and three clues Open case For families 1 min read An old real-photo postcard of a station somewhere in the valley. Can you name the town? Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email The mystery card, with its caption cut off and the station sign blurred. A small wooden depot. A water tower on iron legs. A field of tall grass, and not one person in sight. The card’s caption has been cut off, and the station sign blurred. Clue one. The railroad here was the Michigan Central’s Air Line, which ran from Jackson to Niles. Clue two. The town is in Cass County, east of Cassopolis. Clue three. The Air Line came through in 1871, and the station was set up the same year. Show the answer Vandalia. The caption at the foot of the card reads “R.R. Station Vandalia Mich.” The town’s other cards show the same depot with a train at the platform, and with passengers and a baggage cart. The Air Line between Jackson and Niles was abandoned in 1937. t: Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets
x: ← Front page · All the news Old Cassopolis Where Kellogg made its telephone cabinets Series · 3 of 4 › 2 min read For years the oak cases of Kellogg telephones and switchboards were made in Cassopolis. An old postcard shows the plant, the lumber stacked by the railroad, and the words “Cabinet Shops” painted on the wall. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 2 min read Share Facebook X Email Kellogg Switchboard & Supply Co, Cassopolis, Mich., about 1908–1916, published by O. L. Yerty, Cassopolis. David V. Tinder Collection of Michigan Photography, William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan. Cassopolis, Mich. The card is a real photograph. Long stacks of sawn boards lie in the grass in front, a flatcar stands on the siding, and behind the tracks rise the long, many-windowed buildings of the Kellogg Switchboard & Supply Co. A chimney smokes. On the nearest wall, if you look closely, are the words “Cabinet Shops.” Documented The company was a Chicago maker of telephones and switchboards, founded in 1897. In August 1906 a Paw Paw newspaper reported that Kellogg would put its new woodworking department in Cassopolis. The citizens of the village were to turn over the land and buildings of the late Cassopolis Drill Co., and the title would pass to Kellogg once it had spent an agreed sum on labour and additions. Documented The plant grew. In 1909 the trade journal Telephony counted seven buildings with 46,000 square feet. In November 1910 the company filed papers at Lansing for its Cassopolis woodworking plant and said it had a $75,000 plant there, where “the cabinet work for Kellogg switchboards and telephones” was made. By 1915 there were eight buildings, two warehouses and a dry kiln. Documented In April 1917 the South Bend News-Times reported seventy men at work and six more wanted. There were orders from Italy, from the Dutch East Indies and from the Russian government, and some departments worked until nine at night. That August Telephony walked its readers through an eight-acre plant with a two-acre lumber yard, where tiers of oak waited for the kiln and a new building was going up. Reading The work did not stop with the war. A Kellogg advertising budget printed in Printers’ Ink in 1929 still lists taxes for “Chicago & Cassopolis.” Open When did the Cassopolis plant close, and what stands on its ground today? Where exactly were the old drill works? If you know, or if you have a Kellogg telephone with a Cassopolis case, write to research@projectscroll.com . Enjoyed this story?
