t: Who was in town in 1860?
x: ← Front page · All the news Names on the old maps Who was in town in 1860? From the archive 1 min read 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search. Project Scroll · 22 October 2026 · 1 min read Share Facebook X Email The Cassopolis directory beside the village plan, 1860 wall map. Library of Congress. The St. Joseph River valley. Beside each town plan on the old county maps, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed. Now 331 of those entries, from Cassopolis, Dowagiac, Niles and Paw Paw in 1860 and Goshen in 1861, are in one roll you can search by surname, trade or town, together with the 85 men of Company D. A directory is not a census. It lists the people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not in it. But a directory line puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year, and that is often the first step to finding a family. Every entry links to its map, so you can find the name in the engraving yourself. Enjoyed this story? Pass it on Know someone who grew up around here, or who loves a good mystery? Send it their way. t: The True Northerner, 1 February 1899
x: ← Project Scroll Newspaper of the month The True Northerner, 1 February 1899 One page of an old valley paper, read slowly. This month: the back page of Paw Paw’s weekly, in the middle of a Michigan winter, with egg prices, a farmers’ meeting and the war with Spain at the opera house. The True Northerner was the weekly of Paw Paw, the seat of Van Buren County. Its back page that week was a working page: the market report, the end of a long account of a farmers’ institute, the circuit court, real-estate sales, and the advertisements that paid for it all. Tap any clipping to see it at full size, or open the whole page at the Library of Congress. Our local markets This is what Paw Paw dealers paid farmers that week, not what the shops charged. Butter 12 cents (a pound), eggs 14 cents (a dozen), potatoes 25 cents and wheat 65 cents (a bushel). The units were so well known that the paper did not print them. Cattle and hogs were priced by the pound, “on foot” (alive) or dressed. Above the list, the corner of an advertisement for Royal Baking Powder: “Absolutely Pure,” seven years before the Pure Food and Drug Act. The farmers vote A winter farmers’ institute in Van Buren County passed these resolutions. Senators “should be elected by the people”: in 1899 state legislatures still chose them, and the Seventeenth Amendment did not change that until 1913. County officers should draw a salary instead of keeping fees. And fruit should carry “the name and address of the shipper,” an early demand for honest labels from the fruit belt. A dollar a bushel A. S. Packard of Covert, “one of the most successful peach growers in the county,” told the institute that his last crop came to about 3,000 bushels and averaged him over a dollar a bushel. Peaches were the money crop of the Michigan fruit belt, and the paper promised to print his paper in full. At what age should a child read? The evening session argued about schools. The institute’s president thought a child should be in the second reader by five or six “if it were not for the laziness of parents.” Alice Bangs disagreed: no child ought to begin before six. The paper calls her Miss in one line and Mrs. in the next; the rest of the report says the audience nodded with her. The war at the opera house Six months after the fighting with Spain ended, a travelling company brought moving pictures of it to Longwell’s opera house for one night, Saturday, 4 February. The Lumière cinématographe had been shown for the first time only four years before. Many “war films” of the day were staged re-enactments, so the audience could not always tell what was real. Admission was 10 and 20 cents. Every soldier, life size The advertisement across the foot of the page made the real promise: the reviews of the Michigan volunteer regiments would show “every soldier from Paw Paw and vicinity life size so that each and every one can readily be recognized.” Another notice on the page says that at Grand Rapids parents saw sons who had since been buried in Cuba. Saw edges Men wore detachable starched collars, and a badly ironed one left a rough edge that cut the neck. The Model Steam Laundry on South Kalamazoo Street claimed to be the only laundry in southern Michigan that could take the “saw edges” off. Read the page yourself What did a Paw Paw dealer pay for a dozen eggs? 14 cents. Who chose United States senators in 1899? The state legislatures. Direct election came with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913. How many bushels of peaches did Mr. Packard grow? About 3,000, at over a dollar a bushel. What was showing at Longwell’s opera house on 4 February? Moving pictures of the Spanish-American War, by a Lumière cinématographe company. Reading an old paper Start with the ads and the markets. They tell you what things cost, who kept which shop, and what people wanted to buy. Read the “continued from” stories. The front page opens a story; the back page often holds the names. Do not trust the typed text. The searchable text

t: Niles, Michigan history and records
x: ← The places Berrien County, Michigan Niles, Michigan: its history, in the record Niles stands on the St. Joseph River beside the site of Fort St. Joseph: a Jesuit mission of 1691 and a French fort of 1697, and four flags have flown there — French, British, Spanish and American — which is why the city calls itself the City of Four Flags. The present town was settled in 1827 and named for Hezekiah Niles, the Baltimore newspaper editor. The town at a glance Founded: the mission 1691, the fort 1697; the town settled 1827; village 1835; city 1859. Name: for Hezekiah Niles (1777–1839), editor of Niles’ Weekly Register. In the record: the Fort St. Joseph archaeological project of Western Michigan University; Ellis’s history of Berrien and Van Buren counties (1880) and Coolidge’s of Berrien (1906); the Niles Republican and Niles Democrat. On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley county map’s Niles inset shows the river through the plan; lay it over today’s streets . Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. From “One Letter, Two Certificates.” Read the whole case · All field notes Person of the month · October James M. Shepard, the dentist who wrote it down He was three years old in 1846, when the joke lodge was founded. He came to Cassopolis in 1868 and worked there as a dentist. In September 1870 the village’s reading room was organized in his dental office, and a year later he was one of the incorporators of its library association. When Howard Rogers wrote the county’s first history in 1875, it was Shepard who wrote down the story of the lodge: the halters, the blindfolds, the ball and the two hundred badges. Seven years later, Alfred Mathews reprinted it and named him in a footnote. On the record: in the same winter of 1846–47 that the joke lodge held its ball, the Odd Fellows’ Cass County Lodge No. 21 received its dispensation; Rogers called it “the first legitimate secret society.” The open question. He was three in 1846. Who told him? Sources: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), pp. 253–254 and 258; A. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174. t: One Letter, Two Certificates
x: ← All field notes Field notes · No. 1 · 17 October 2026 One Letter, Two Certificates One letter. That’s all it was. A single middle initial, and it nearly turned one man into two. The case A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. The old county histories give him a plain first and last name. One of them adds “Senior.” County history His own death certificate, filed about a month after he died, gives the same plain name. No initial at all. Document Then we found his son’s death certificate, from 1935. In the box for the father’s name, whoever answered the questions gave him a middle initial: the same one the son carried. Document So which is right? Make your guess now. Ours is further down. Then it got stranger Once we started comparing every box, the records kept arguing. His birthday: his death certificate and one of the county histories are two days apart. His father’s birthplace: the certificate names one state. That same history names another. One man, one family and three disagreements. Nobody lied. Each one is somebody’s memory. What this teaches Every record was written by someone. A death certificate tells you what the informant believed, on a hard day. Their name is usually on it. The father’s was filed about a month after he died; the son’s was filled in twenty-three years later, by someone remembering a man long gone. County histories have the same weakness: the family usually supplied the facts, often from memory, and nobody checked them. One letter can change everything. Fathers and sons with the same name get tangled in the record all the time. One wrong initial can merge two men or split one, and send you chasing somebody else’s family for a month. Watch out for “Senior.” In the 1800s it didn’t always mean “father.” Sometimes it only meant the older of two men with the same name in town, related or not. Here a son with the same name does turn up, so the label fits, but always check. Disagreement is a clue, not a failure. Every mismatch tells you who was remembering, and when. Our guess, as promised: father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . But a guess is not proof. Four rules for when records disagree Ask who gave the information, and when. Closer to the event usually weighs more, but not always. Keep looking. A third, independent record can tip the balance, but records are weighed, not counted. Write down both versions and where each came from. Never quietly “fix” one. Call it settled only when the evidence settles it. Until then, it’s an open question. Where the case stands Open Our next witness: a local newspaper notice from the days or weeks after his death. Then his probate file, and the cemetery’s burial records or a transcription of his stone. Read the stone on paper. Don’t go to it. Scrollmarks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — what the marks mean Where to look, for free Archives of Michigan, death certificates 1897–1952 . Free; for most years you can open the certificate itself, in the original handwriting. FamilySearch . Birth, marriage and death records from all over the world, free with an account. Michiganology: vital records . The State of Michigan’s own index to its births, marriages and deaths. Michigan County Histories and Atlases . The University of Michigan’s free scans of the county histories, Rogers, Mathews and Glover among them. Find a Grave . Free transcriptions and photographs of gravestones. Read the stone on paper. Tip: read every box, including the small print at the bottom. Ages are often given to the day, in years, months and days. Count back from the date of death and you have a birth date to check against everything else. Just remember the informant gave that age too. x: ← Visit & Plan Outdoors & water Beaches, rivers, trails and orchards The valley is made of water: Lake Michigan on one side, the St. Joseph River through the middle, and lakes in every township. Here are the public beaches, parks, rail-trails and water trails, the u-pick orchards and the wine trail, with when to go, what it costs and whether the dog can come. Beaches and lake access 13 Lake Michigan’s sand and the inland lakes’ swimming beaches. Michigan state parks need a Recreation Passport on the car; Indiana state parks charge at the gate. Beach / state park · Sawyer, MI Warren Dunes State Park Lake Michigan beach under some of the tallest dunes on the shore; swim in the buoyed area, climb Tower Hill, or walk six miles of wooded trails. Paddleboard and kayak rentals in summer. When: Open all year; beach season Memorial Day to Labor Day; cross-country skiing listed as a winter activity. Phone 269-426-4013. Cost: Michigan Recreation Passport required for vehicle entry (nonresident day pass $12, annual $42; residents $15 with plate renewal). Dogs: Yes, on a 6-foot leash, on the beach north of the northernmost swim buoy (about 2.5 miles of shoreline). Access: Three accessible restroom buildings in the beach day-use area; three 100-foot accessible walkways toward the water (they stop short of the water's edge); two beach wheelchairs to borrow at the ranger station. The story: Businessman Edward K. Warren bought the dunes and beach as a conservation measure; the land became a state park in 1930. Source 12032 Red Arrow Highway, Sawyer, MI 49125 Official page · Directions Beach / state park / dunes · Stevensville, MI Grand Mere State Park Hike over wooded dunes to about half a mile of quiet Lake Michigan shoreline, or fish for bluegill on South and Middle lakes; a fine spring birding spot. When: Open all year; snowshoeing in winter. Vault toilets and a picnic pavilion by the main lot. Cost: Michigan Recreation Passport (vehicle entry). Dogs: Yes, on a 6-foot leash, along the half mile of Lake Michigan shoreline. The story: Its three inland lakes, remnants of five, formed as the glaciers retreated; the area was named a National Natural Landmark in 1968. t: Paw Paw, Michigan history and records
x: ← The places Van Buren County, Michigan Paw Paw, Michigan: its history, in the record Paw Paw, the seat of Van Buren County, takes its name from the Paw Paw River and the pawpaw trees that grew along it. Rodney Hinckley took up a farm on the river in 1832, a sawmill followed in 1833, and the village was incorporated in 1837; the Van Buren County Courthouse on Paw Paw Street is on the National Register of Historic Places. The town at a glance Founded: settled 1832–33; incorporated 1837; the county seat. Name: from the Paw Paw River, itself named for the pawpaw tree. In the record: Ellis’s history of Berrien and Van Buren counties (1880) and Rowland’s of Van Buren (1912); the Paw Paw True Northerner, from the 1850s. On the map: the 1860 Geil & Harley county map carries a plan of Paw Paw; lay it over today’s streets . Wine country: grapes are the district’s crop; St. Julian and Warner Vineyards both began in Paw Paw, and the village holds a Wine and Harvest Festival each autumn. t: Old postcards and photographs of the valley
x: ← The map room Postcards, then and now Stand where the photographer stood Old postcards of Cassopolis, from the days of wagons to the first motor cars. Each one was taken from a spot you can still stand on. Find it, take the same picture today, and send it to us: we will set your photograph beside the old one here, with your name on it. West side of Broadway, looking south. A Yerty postcard. The photographer stood on Broadway with the stores of the west side on the right. Find it on the 1860 plan → Broadway in the days of wagons. Horses and wagons on the main street, the store fronts close together. Find it on the 1860 plan → Carriages drawn up on Broadway. A row of buggies at the hitching rail: a market day, or a meeting. Find it on the 1860 plan → Broadway when the first cars came. Early motor cars among the last of the buggies. Find it on the 1860 plan → A Cassopolis street, early 1900s. Which street is it? The trees, the walks and the buildings are the clues. Find it on the 1860 plan → The road to town. The way in from the country. Where did it come in, and is the road still there? Find it on the 1860 plan → How to rephotograph a postcard Find the spot. Line up two things that have not moved, a corner of a building and a street, and walk until they sit in the picture the way they sit on the card. Match the height. Most old postcards were taken from about head height; some from an upstairs window. Hold the camera where the photographer’s eye was. Match the lens. Use your phone’s ordinary camera, not the wide one, and do not zoom. Stay safe and on public ground. Never step into the road for a shot, and never go onto private property without leave. Send it in to research@projectscroll.com , saying which card and when you took it. By sending it you let us show it here with your name. The pictures are taken from old postcards of Cassopolis. Each was published before 1931, or published without a copyright notice, and is in the public domain in the United States. The pairings will be added as readers send them in. Then and now: your photographs The first pair is waiting for you. Take the same picture as one of these postcards, from the same spot, and send it in. Your photograph will go here beside the old one, with a slider to move between then and now, and your name under it. The valley on old postcards and photographs 121 more views of the towns of the St. Joseph River valley, from Cassopolis to Michigan City: main streets, depots, courthouses, libraries, hotels, mills, fairs and parades, most of them between 1900 and 1930. Each one links to the library or archive that holds it. Press a picture to see it full size. t: Privacy
x: ← Project Scroll Privacy What this site keeps Almost nothing. Project Scroll has no accounts and no ads of its own. One thing is optional and off until you say yes: a visit counter from Meta, used to see how the hunt is found and, later, to show Project Scroll’s own advertisements to people who have been here. You choose on your first visit, and you can change your mind here. Your choice on this device: not made yet Kept in your own browser A few things are remembered so the site works the way you left it. They are stored in your browser on this device, nobody else can see them, and we never receive them. Light or dark. The page colors you chose. The lantern. Whether you put it out. The opening flourish. That you have already seen the ink draw itself on your first visit, so it does not replay. Your tin badges. The badges you have earned around the site, and the days you visited, so the “Regular” badge can count them. Your followed cases. The cases you starred on the case board. Your case notes. Anything you write in a case notebook. See all your notes . Your answer about the visit counter. Allow or keep off, so you are not asked again. Your drafts. What you type into the message form and the family-history and family-legend forms, so it survives a reload. Nothing is sent from those forms; you copy the text and send it yourself. To clear all of it, clear this site’s data in your browser settings. Sent to other sites Where am I? On a then-and-now page, the “Where am I?” button asks your device for its location so it can put a dot on the old plan. The location is used only in your browser, to draw the dot. It is never sent to Project Scroll or stored. Maps. The modern map under the site’s maps (town names, highways, streets and aerial photographs) comes from the USGS National Map, a free public-domain service of the US Geological Survey. While a map is open, your browser asks the USGS server (basemap.nationalmap.gov) for its map pieces, so that server sees your internet address, as any website would, under the USGS privacy policies . No account, cookie or tracking is involved. Choose “Plain” or “Lines” on a map to use only what the site itself draws. The map room. The 1860 wall map is shown straight from the Library of Congress, so your browser asks the Library’s image server (tile.loc.gov) for the pieces of the map you look at. The other county maps in the map room come the same way from the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Libraries (cdm17272.contentdm.oclc.org) and the University of Michigan Library (quod.lib.umich.edu). The Sanborn sheets and the Cassopolis page’s 1884 corner come from Wikimedia Commons (commons.wikimedia.org and its image servers). The 1860 half of the Penn Township slider on the Cassopolis page comes from the same server. Facebook. Links to Project Scroll’s Facebook pages and Messenger simply take you there. On a case page you can choose to show the live Facebook post; only then does your browser load it from Facebook, under Facebook’s own terms. Until you click, nothing from Facebook is loaded. The Meta visit counter (only if you allow it). If you choose “Allow”, your browser loads a small script from Meta (the Meta Pixel) that tells Meta which pages of this site you looked at, and when. Meta may match that to a Facebook or Instagram account if you have one, under Meta’s privacy policy . We use it to see which parts of the hunt and the studio are visited, and later to show Project Scroll’s own advertisements on Facebook and Instagram to people who have been here. It records page views, when the Services section is read, and when the Messenger button is pressed. It never sees what you type: your notes, drafts and messages stay in your browser as before. If you choose “Keep it off”, or make no choice, nothing from Meta is loaded, and nothing is counted. When you write to us Email to research@projectscroll.com lands in a mailbox hosted for us by GoDaddy on Microsoft 365, under GoDaddy’s privacy policy ; mess

t: Genealogy and local history research, Michigan and Indiana
x: ← Project Scroll Professional services Genealogy and local history research services, Michigan and Indiana Project Scroll’s research desk takes commissions: a lost ancestor traced, a family history or register built from original records, a family legend tested against the record, or local history research for an author, a film or a community group. Based in the St. Joseph River Valley of southwest Michigan and northern Indiana, working anywhere the records reach. What we research Lost ancestors. One clear question, answered from certificates, deeds, censuses, county histories, maps and newspapers, every statement marked with its source. Family histories and registers. Every descendant of one couple, or every ancestor of one person, built from the records and written to be checked. See a specimen . Family legends tested. The famous ancestor, the three brothers who came over together, the land that was taken. We find where the story began and what the records say. How it works . Local history for authors, films and groups. Research to a brief, with a sourced report you own. A second pair of eyes. A manuscript, chapter or article checked against its sources before it goes out. Where we work Cass, Berrien, Van Buren and St. Joseph counties in Michigan; St. Joseph and Elkhart counties in Indiana; and, wherever the records are online, anywhere. We read the Michigan county histories, the General Land Office tract books and plats, Michigan and Indiana vital records, and the newspapers of the St. Joseph River Valley as a matter of course. How a commission works Tell us what you have. A name, a place, rough dates and what the family says. The form lays it out. An honest first read, free. We tell you what the records are likely to show, and what it will take, before you commit to anything. The work, marked. Every claim cited; every gap written down beside what was found. You own the report. Nothing about your family is published or shared without your word. t: How the valley was joined
x: ← The map room Roads, rails, bridges and mills How the valley was joined First came the canals that were never dug and the plank roads that were. Then the bridges over the St. Joseph, and at last the iron road, which decided which towns would grow and which would wait. Here it is in the order it happened, each date from the county histories with its page. The dates 26 March 1835 Niles. A charter was granted to Obed P. Lacey for a toll bridge over the St. Joseph at Niles. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 8 December 1835 Niles. A public meeting at Niles called for a free bridge at Main Street. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 2 February 1836 Edwardsburg. Citizens met at Edwardsburg about a canal from Constantine to Niles; most of those present favored a railroad. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 79 21 March 1836 Niles. Niles obtained a charter for a free bridge across the St. Joseph River. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 26 March 1836 Constantine. The Legislature incorporated the Constantine and Niles Canal or Railroad Company. Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 79 24 May 1845 Niles. The contract to build the Broadway bridge at Niles was let to Henry J. Holmes. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 159 3 April 1848 Paw Paw. The act incorporating the Paw Paw Plank-Road Company was approved. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 50 7 October 1848 Niles. The Michigan Central Railroad was completed to Niles, and the first passenger train from Detroit arrived. Mathews (1882, p. 80) gives the same date. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 53 22 March 1849 Niles. The Niles and Mottville plank-road company was incorporated. (Berrien and Van Buren history, 1880, p. 50, gives the same date.) Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 77 12 July 1851 Niles. The first through train from Lake Erie reached South Bend, creating great excitement. History of St. Joseph County, Indiana (Chapman, 1880), p. 456 4 January 1869 Niles. The new iron bridge over the St. Joseph River at Niles was completed and accepted by the city's Board of Aldermen. History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties, Michigan (D. W. Ensign, 1880), p. 160 2 February 1870 St. Joseph. The railroad from St. Joseph to New Buffalo opened for traffic, and St. Joseph held a grand celebration. t: Scrollmarks: how we mark the evidence
x: ← Project Scroll · Discoveries · Lore and legends How we mark the evidence Scrollmarks™ Not every source is worth the same. A death certificate filed the week a man died is not a story his grandson told sixty years later, and neither of them is our own opinion. Scrollmarks are the nine marks Project Scroll puts on every statement in its research, strongest first, so you can see at a glance what the record says and what we are arguing from it. Strongest Weakest What the record says What we argue from it What the record says Document Made at the time, by someone whose job was to write it down: a death certificate, a deed, a census page, a survey, a map. Example: a 1912 Michigan death certificate. Period print Printed at or near the time: a newspaper notice, an obituary, a book of the day. Example: a doctor’s obituary printed the year he died. County history The big county histories of the 1870s to the 1910s. Rich and indispensable, but often written decades later from what families remembered, and rarely checked. Example: the 1882 History of Cass County. Compiled A later hand gathering earlier records: an index, a bibliography, a transcription, a modern summary. Good for finding things; we go back to the original whenever it survives. Example: a trail-diary bibliography that lists an unpublished typescript. Tradition What a family or a community says, passed down by word of mouth. Worth recording exactly as told, and worth testing. Example: “Grandpa always said he came over on the last boat before the war.” Field What we saw or measured ourselves, at first hand, dated, from public ground or with permission. Example: a dated photograph of a marker on a public roadside. What we argue from it Inference A step that follows directly from the records. Example: one certificate was filed a month after he died, the other twenty-three years later, so the first informant was closer to the event. Reading Our interpretation of what the records point to. Always labeled, always open to correction. Example: “In 1935, someone gave the father his son’s initial.” Hypothesis An idea worth testing that the records don’t yet support. We say what would prove or disprove it. Example: he never used a middle initial at all; his obituary and gravestone would tell. Marks, strongest first: Document Period print County history Compiled Tradition Field (seen at first hand) Inference Reading Hypothesis — the last three marks are our own argument, offered for correction How it looks in a report A pioneer died in Michigan in 1912. His death certificate gives no middle initial Document . A county history adds “Senior” to his name County history . His son’s death certificate, filled in twenty-three years later, gives the father a middle initial: the son’s own Document . The first informant was closer to the event Inference . Father and son shared a name, and in 1935 someone gave the father the son’s initial too Reading . Or he never used a middle initial at all, which his obituary would show Hypothesis . Tap a mark to see what it means. From our case “ One Letter, Two Certificates .” Every report you receive from us is marked the same way. Weigh the evidence Add records to each side and watch the scale. Records are weighed, not counted: one good document can outweigh a pile of family stories. Side A Side B The scale is level. Add a record to either side. The weights are a rule of thumb, not a formula: a late or careless document can still be wrong, and a detailed tradition can still be right. Try marking these yourself Teachers and group leaders are welcome to use this exercise and the hunter’s worksheet in class. Tell us how it went. Pick the mark you would give each one. A notice in the local paper, the week after he died. Period print. It was printed at the time, but by a newspaper, not by an office whose job was to record the death. “Great-aunt Ruth always said the family came from Ohio.” Tradition. Write it down exactly as she said it, then go and test it. A

x: ← Project Scroll Soldiers of the valley Company D, Sixth Michigan Infantry In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County. Here are its 85 men as the county history printed them in 1882: who they were, how they served, and how 19 of them did not come home. The company’s war Raised at Dowagiac, summer 1861, under Capt. Charles E. Clarke, with Frederick J. Clarke as first lieutenant. The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. Mathews, p. 117 Baltimore, then the Mississippi. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge on 5 August 1862, and in the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick Clarke was killed. pp. 117–118 Heavy artillery. After Port Hudson the regiment became heavy artillery, served at Fort Morgan and in the siege of Mobile, and was paid off and discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865. p. 118 Of the men below, 4 were killed or died of wounds and 15 died of disease: at Baltimore, New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Carrollton and, most of all, in the hot summer at Port Hudson. Disease killed more soldiers than battle in this war, and this company is no exception. t: The sources shelf
x: ← Project Scroll The sources shelf What the hunt is built on Every clue on Project Scroll comes from a book, a map or a record you can open yourself. Here they are on one shelf, with where to read each one free and a plain word on how far to trust it. New: The libraries behind the stories : every library, archive and newspaper our news stories draw on, and which stories use each one. County histories How far to trust them. Written a generation or two after the events, mostly from the recollections of old settlers, and paid for by subscribers whose biographies they print. Rich in names and dates, wrong often enough that every fact should be checked against a deed, a census or a newspaper. Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (Cassopolis: W. H. Mansfield, 1875). University of Michigan Library The earliest county history, closest to the first settlers. Short, and often the source the later books copy. Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago: Waterman, Watkins & Co., 1882). University of Michigan Library Much longer, with township and village histories and biographies. Repeats Rogers in places, adds new witnesses in others; its footnotes say who told what. L. H. Glover, A Twentieth Century History of Cass County, Michigan (Chicago: Lewis Publishing, 1906). University of Michigan Library The county as it stood a generation later. Good on churches, schools and businesses of its day; leans on the earlier books for the pioneer years. Portrait and Biographical Record of Berrien and Cass Counties, Michigan (Chicago: Biographical Publishing Co., 1893). Subscription biographies, written with the families. Strong on births, marriages and children; kind to its subjects. County and town maps How far to trust them. Landownership maps were sold by subscription, so the names on the farms and the directories beside the town plans are the people who paid. The streets, lots and buildings are usually true to the ground; the names are a snapshot of one year. Geil, Harley & Siverd, Map of the Counties of Cass, Van Buren and Berrien, Michigan (Philadelphia, 1860). Library of Congress The wall map at the heart of the map room, with its town plans and business directories. Map of St. Joseph County, Michigan (1858). Library of Congress The neighbouring county two years earlier: Three Rivers, Constantine, Centreville, White Pigeon. Geil & Harley, Map of Kalamazoo County, Michigan (1861). Library of Congress Kalamazoo, Portage, Schoolcraft and the ground where Vicksburg grew. M. W. Stokes, Map of St. Joseph Co., Indiana (South Bend, 1863). Library of Congress South Bend and Lowell, Mishawaka and the townships, with engraved views. Geil & Harley, Map of Elkhart Co. Indiana (Philadelphia: Samuel Geil, 1861). American Geographical Society Library, University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Goshen, Elkhart, Bristol, Middlebury and the farms between. W. W. Graves, Atlas of Berrien County, Michigan (Chicago: Rand McNally). University of Michigan Library Township plates with every farm, from Benton to Three Oaks. R. L. Polk & Co., Illustrated Historical Atlas of Kent County, Michigan (1894). University of Michigan Library Grand Rapids Township and the city’s edge. Plat book of Cass County, Michigan (about 1928). scans contributed by Ross Traverse to the Cass County MIGenWeb Project The township sheets of about 1928, for following a farm from 1860 to the age of the automobile. Views, plans and insurance maps How far to trust them. Bird’s-eye views were drawn to sell a town, so they flatter it, but the streets and big buildings are carefully placed. t: St. Joseph, Michigan: history and records
x: ← Visit & Plan Berrien County, Michigan St. Joseph St. Joseph sits on the bluff where the St. Joseph River meets Lake Michigan. La Salle built Fort Miami near here in the winter of 1679, and William Burnett kept a trading post at the river mouth from about 1780. Calvin Britain and Augustus Newell took up land in 1829, and the village they laid out was first called Newburyport. It was incorporated as St. Joseph in 1834, became a city in 1891, and in 1894 took the county seat from Berrien Springs. At a glance Founded land claimed by Calvin Britain and Augustus B. Newell, 1829; post office 1831, with Britain as first postmaster; village of St. Joseph incorporated March 7, 1834; city, June 5, 1891 Name for the river. Ellis's 1880 county history records that the place was first called Newburyport, and the probate court dated its papers "Newburyport (St. Joseph)" until 1837 The fruit port Ellis tells of seedling peaches from B. C. Hoyt's garden shipped across the lake to Chicago in 1839; once the timber trade waned, fruit became the port's chief export Industry in 1911 the Upton brothers began making electric washing machines in St. Joseph; the business became the Whirlpool Corporation County seat yes, of Berrien County since 1894, when a county vote moved the seat from Berrien Springs Worth a visit St. Joseph North Pier Inner and Outer Lights , North pier, mouth of the St. Joseph River, St. Joseph. The two lighthouses on the north pier at the river mouth, joined by a catwalk; walk out the pier. National Register, 2005. Ninth District Lighthouse Depot , 128 N. Pier St., St. Joseph. The old lighthouse service depot on the pier. National Register, 1993. Whitcomb Hotel , 509 Ship St., St. Joseph. The downtown hotel tower above the lake. National Register, 2021. Blossomland Bridge , M-63 over the St. Joseph River. The bascule bridge carrying M-63 over the St. Joseph River between St. Joseph and Benton Harbor. National Register, 1999. Where the records are St. Joseph is the county seat, but Berrien County's older vital records are kept by the County Records Department at 2100 E. Empire Ave., Benton Township: births and deaths from 1867, marriages from 1831; birth records over 100 years old are open. The Maud Preston Palenske Memorial Library in St. Joseph keeps a local history room. The Heritage Museum & Cultural Center on Main Street has archival collections and a research library. The St. Joseph Traveler, Herald and Herald-Press run from 1859 into the 1970s, much of it digitized on Newspapers.com and NewspaperArchive (subscription). Ellis's History of Berrien and Van Buren Counties (1880) gives the town a full chapter. t: Front Street Virtual Walk
x: ← Project Scroll Front Street Virtual Walk Walk old Front Street Dowagiac, Michigan, the stove town: 13 stops through the downtown that the Round Oak works, the lure makers and the railroad built, each with what stood there and what is there now. Walk it from your chair, or bring this page to Front Street and stamp each stop on the spot. The map opens here. 1860 plan Dowagiac’s 1860 plan over today’s streets Also: Broadway, Cassopolis › Every stop Stop 1 of 13 Dowagiac Area History Museum Then. The town's history museum began at Southwestern Michigan College and moved downtown in 2013, taking over a building that had held retail shops. Its biggest story is the Round Oak Stove Company, which Philo D. Beckwith incorporated in 1871 after casting his first stove around 1867 to heat his own foundry; the company stopped making stoves in 1946 and its buildings were sold in 1947. Now. A free museum (Tuesday-Friday 10-5, Saturday 10-2) with about 4,000 square feet of exhibits, including what is described as the largest public collection of Round Oak heating stoves in the world. 201 E. Division St., Dowagiac, MI 49047 source 1 source 2 source 3 source 4 source 5 source 6 · Open the Sanborn sheets of Dowagiac Stop 2 of 13 The Heddon Museum Then. The museum tells the story of James Heddon, who in the late 1890s whittled a piece of wood while waiting by the Mill Pond, saw a bass strike it when he tossed it in, and went on to make a top-water lure he named the Dowagiac. James Heddon's Sons ran from 1902 to 1984 and by the 1920s was the world's biggest maker of quality fishing tackle, also turning out golf shafts, ski poles, violin bows, box kites and, in World War II, radio antennae. Now. A volunteer-run museum of the Dowagiac Area History Museum (open Tuesday and Friday, 10-5; call ahead) with more than 1,000 lures, 140 reels and 150 rods. 115 S. Open park ground from 1848, this corner became the site of the Beckwith Memorial in 1892, built in memory of Round Oak founder P. D. Beckwith by his daughter and son-in-law, in Lake Superior red sandstone, and dedicated in January 1893. Besides a 600-seat theatre counted among the finest between New York and Chicago, the building held a bank, city hall and the Round Oak company offices; films were shown from 1914. It was torn down in 1966, and a bank building later stood on part of the lot; the city bought that in 2019, took it down in 2020 and added the ground to the park. Now. Beckwith Park, renovated and reopened in July 2021. A piece of the theatre's red sandstone wall still shows on the building next door. Southeast corner of S.
